results.title: "You can never see outside of yourself": The House Before is a body horror game in which you are a house tunnelling through its own soul
results.author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell
results.content:
It's a lovely morning in the village, and you are a horrible house. Wait, let's start that again. As Gregor Samsa awoke one morning from uneasy dreams he found himself transformed into a horrible house. Wait, let's start that again: "You wake up as a House. Your limbs stretch through endless rooms filled with grotesque creatures. You can never see outside of yourself, never feel the world that lies beyond the fleshy walls of your body. You manage your insides as best you can, but you wonder: are you a good house or just a pale afterthought of the House Before?"
So goes the blurb for The House Before, an atypical body horror game from Gabriel Helfenstein and the art collective Fantasia Malware, which combines elements from visual novels and text adventure with a lot of lurid minigames. It's a journey through your own architectural guts that appears to span a variety of genres: first-person maze games, virtual pet games, top-down tile-based exploration. There are also some bespoke, eminently proddable interface designs that make me think of 90s game installers and virtual desktop music players.
The opening suggestion of being trapped inside your own form is wonderfully claustrophobic, but this seems like lighthearted pastiche in other respects. The creatures you'll meet are both garrulous and colourful. I swore never to idly compare things to vapo(u)rwave again, but I cannot deny the innermost yearnings of my soul: the aesthetics are quite vapo(u)rwavey in places. Look at those shimmering, oily pinks and purples on the "clock" screen. At other times, it's less of a shimmer, more of an ooze, and I think of Nickelodeon. In general, I'm always eager to play games that are ghastly and inventive composites.
The House Before is out November on Steam and Itch.io (the latter's store page isn't yet live as of writing). "If you enjoy short stories such as The Red Tower by Thomas Ligotti or games such as Growing My Grandpa! by Yames, The House Before is for you," notes a press release.
Here is what Alice O (RPS in peace) wrote about Growing My Grandpa!, back in 2024: "You can feed him everything a grandpa needs to grow up strong and healthy: stale cashews, brown bananas, fibreglass insulation, the usual grandpa foods. And absolutely you can even talk with your dear grandpa, once he grows a mouth." Here is a complementary gobbet from Ligotti's The Red Tower: "We are all talking and thinking about the Red Tower in our own degenerate way. I have only recorded what everyone is saying (though they may not know they are saying it), and sometimes what they have seen (though they may not know they have seen it)."
The press release adds that The House Before "won't be for everyone", even though it'll be pretty short at a few hours. I don't know what they're on about. Who wouldn't want to be the absolute worst house? If you prefer your houses to be more cheerful and flirtatious, there's always Building Relationships.
Helfenstein's previous games include North, from way back in 2016. Janksta backstabber Brendy (RPS in peace, grudgingly) wrote about North in one of his free game round-ups, which harbours a few other specimens of note.
results.summary:
Developer Gabriel Helfenstein and art collective Fantasia Malware are set to release The House Before, a surreal body horror game where players navigate a sentient, architectural nightmare.

### Key Points
- The House Before launches this November on Steam and Itch.io.
- Gameplay blends visual novel elements, text adventures, and diverse minigames like first-person mazes.
- The game features a distinct aesthetic described as a mix of vaporwave, 90s software interfaces, and Nickelodeon-style visuals.
- It is marketed as a short, experimental experience for fans of surreal horror works like Thomas Ligotti’s The Red Tower.
- The project follows developer Gabriel Helfenstein’s previous title, the 2016 game North.

### Why it Matters
This title represents a growing trend of experimental, short-form indie games that prioritize unique aesthetic experiences over traditional mechanics. By blending disparate genres into a cohesive body horror narrative, the developers are targeting a niche audience interested in unconventional, art-driven interactive storytelling.

results.title: Lotus Notes and the dangers of starting from scratch
results.author: Matthew Guay
results.content:
Lotus Notes, in 1989, had encryption two years before Pretty Good Privacy brought it to normal email, had rich text formatting and attachments before MIME, had read receipts, notifications, a directory of users, and wiki-style cross-message links. It, rightly, felt like the future.
Or like déjà vu, if you’d used email on a timesharing computer at your university.
Lotus Notes was the future of communications, a decade before laptops had WiFi. Yet of all things, it wasn’t even an email app. It was a notes app, a collaboration tool, an all-things-to-all-people software that let you build apps in the way Access and Airtable later would. That, and the notes could be used for email.
Love it or hate it (and there were plenty on both sides of the fence), what you couldn’t do was ignore it. This email-and-everything-else platform showed what the future of digital communications would become — and provoked, as email itself was always doomed to provoke, equal measures of awe and exasperation.
When the future’s staring you in the face
The future started out as a plain text file. In 1973, the University of Illinois’ claim to fame was a state-of-the-art timesharing computer, PLATO, built for education—the computer where the first language learning software was built, among others.
PLATO came with “an open text file called ‘notes’,” recalled then-17-year-old David Woolley. “Anyone could edit the file and add a comment to the end,” as a place to leave pointers or log issues or, less helpfully, note that Kilroy was here or delete the entire note. A bit too flexible for an educational environment.
“It was just such an incident that prompted Tenczar to ask me to develop a replacement,” said Woolley. And so he set out to tame the mess with something better. “Some problems might require back-and-forth conversation between a user and the system staff,” he concluded, and built a tool that’d allow up to 63 responses per note, “chained together in sequence ... so that each note could become the starting point of an ongoing conversation.” And in the end, his PLATO Notes, “named after the text file it replaced,” said Woolley, would be one of the earliest online forums, Reddit before its time.
You could start new discussions, respond to existing ones, and read through the comments. And with Personal Notes, the later expansions on the original idea, you could send email-style personal notes, privately, to anyone else. All in a synced database, accessed through individual terminals, in something that offered “a peek at what the Internet would ultimately become,” alum Ray Ozzie told the New York Times after having worked on PLATO as a student.
For Ozzie, PLATO Notes enabled early remote work, with him and a coding partner collaborating across different shifts. A reply could drop into a forum with no one there to read it, and it would still be waiting when they came back. Upon entering the workforce after having seen a different future for work, “I started going through ... withdrawal,” recalled Ozzie, when in the real world there was “no online community.”
“After graduation, I said to myself, ‘By hook or crook, I am going to build software to recreate the interactive environment I’d used with Plato,’” Ozzie would later recall.
With hooks into the Lotus team that’d built the Lotus 1-2-3 spreadsheet, and enough time in development hell that the company had to tongue-in-cheek acknowledge the delays (“Notes is coming off the vaporware list,” said a spokesperson when it finally launched in 1989, five years after entering development), Ozzie kept his promise with Lotus Notes.
Notes, that is. Not email, per se.
The everything email app
What you have discovered is a recipe not for memory, but for reminder. ~ Plato
The lessons of PLATO Notes weren’t about email as much as they were about the power of community, of a shared brain, of the power of having everyone’s ideas together in one place. And that was what the Lotus Notes team set out to replicate.
“It was eccentric to think about group communications software in 1984, when most people had never touched an email system,” noted Tom Diaz, former VP of Engineering at Iris.
PLATO Notes gave users the experience of joining in a shared community backed by a synced database, long before the internet. PCs on every desk didn’t change that dynamic; you still needed networking to recreate the same experience. So Lotus Notes was built as a database, one that synced everything with every other computer. “Servers exchanged information through replicated data; there were potentially many copies of the same database resident on different servers, and the Notes server software continuously synchronized them,” IBM explained years later (spoiler alert: Big Blue would acquire Lotus mostly for Notes, in 1995). That means, in the age when checking your email often meant pulling messages one time over POP3, Lotus Notes was keeping messages in sync, for the same experience IMAP and Microsoft Exchange would later provide.
But it wasn’t just email. For email is private messages sent in standards-compliant ways, and Lotus Notes was designed to “pick the brains of everyone in your organization as if they all sat at the next desk,” as Fortune’s David Kirkpatrick described it. “With Notes, everyone puts his contributions onto databases, and you tell the system what kinds of information you want to see.” And so you could have a private message, email-style, or more commonly you could write something publicly that synced across everyone in your company’s database, a corporate version of PLATO Notes’ freewheeling, ad hoc community.
You had something you couldn’t replicate anywhere else, something it’d take Teams and Slack plus email to approximate today. And as a database, you could build anything. Calendars, forums, address books, custom internal software—everything was possible in the app that just happened to also support its own variant of email as almost an afterthought, a showcase of what else you could build in Notes (it wouldn’t support SMTP email until 1996, and by then email had caught up to many of Notes’ advances).
Encryption was baked into Lotus Notes from the start, as part of the database. As was rich text formatting and file attachments, both things normal email wouldn’t get until MIME’s launch in ‘92. You could link to other messages, like a wiki, something email still doesn’t have since each message is a stand-alone text file instead of a shared database. It had a categorized inbox, of sorts, and threaded messages, long before other email apps would. If you didn’t like something, you could fix it and code your own email app from the same database core. And you could take all of your mail with you, syncing whenever you were back on the network, hardly a selling point at first but increasingly a key use case as laptops started entering the workforce.
Those computers might not be running the same operating system, either. So Lotus Notes was cross-platform from day one, originally on DOS and OS/2, later on Windows, Unix, and the Macintosh, complete with its own custom graphical user interface to work consistently across every platform.
And that, the unique interface that looked and worked the same everywhere, was its Achilles’ heel.
Love it or hate it
To the fans, Lotus Notes was like nothing else. Powerful, expandable, feature-rich at a time when email was plain English text. Plus, it wasn’t just email. “Email is about 5% of the actual use of Notes,” one countered on a post about Lotus Notes’ flaws; “Email is just one of the things it does (albeit poorly),” said another.
“Using Notes you could suddenly create applications that shared data across your office locations,” reminisced @andrewstuart on Hacker News. “You ran a server locally and Notes dialed up the other servers and did replication of just the changed/different data. It was gob smacking [sic] because nothing else could do this.”
But it did all of that, while working differently from almost any other application on your computer. Lotus Notes was built for every operating system, in a time when conventions were yet to be set in stone. It forged its own path—and if you were used to it, perhaps that was fine, but for anyone switching between Lotus Notes and other popular software, the differences, the things that’d break your muscle memory, became infuriating over time.
“If I want to ‘refresh’ the inbox shouldn’t I press F5? Nope, that will lock the app and require your password to unlock it,” went one of the many complaints collected on Stack Overflow co-founder Jeff Atwood’s blog. “How do I send an email? CTRL+ENTER? Of course not! ALT+1, naturally.”
The anti-conventions were so bad, there was an entire Lotus Notes Interface Hall of Shame noting, among other things, that you could not have more than eight Lotus Notes windows open at once, that some buttons required a double-click when others required a more conventional single-click, that the spellcheck would check email addresses in the To: field and inevitably suggest that you change them. Lotus Notes, far ahead of its time, would notify you when new mail arrived, a foreshadowing of push notifications. But, the notification had both “OK” and “Open Mail...” buttons—the former would not actually load the new mail, while the latter would but only if the Drafts folder wasn’t open.
Then there was the Lotus Notes Sucks site, detailing over 80 ways the program had driven the author to near-madness. The best? A warning that “You must change your password” that then asked “Do you want to change your password now?” followed by both yes and no buttons. “I give up,” sighed the author.
Its best features were beguiling. You were locked into sharing notes and emailing only inside of your company, at first, but you were sending rich text messages with attachments that notified the recipient upon arrival with colleagues on practically any computer, years before BlackBerries and Slack. It was enough for some to put up with its eccentricities, and once your company ran on Notes, the stream of notifications and shared knowledge in synced databases became difficult to live without. It was hard enough to migrate all of your data away that you might as well stick with it (as some still do, in its latest incarnation as HCL Notes).
A powerful tool, yes. A great email application, no. For all of Ozzie’s fond memories of PLATO Notes’ forums and collaboration, it was mail that would stick with us for the long haul — and shape how Notes was judged. “The first implementation most people saw of it was the email side, and it could be a truly clunky and unpleasant email client,” noted @dspillett. “This soured opinions before people delved into the document management and programmability features that email handling were just one use of.”
And while it was advanced at launch, it was slow to adapt to the rapidly changing world. Its email was an island unto itself until 1996, long after most of the world had moved on to SMTP. “The engineers could never manage to get out of their programming mindsets and build the thing to do what users want,” noted Aaron Lawrence, “and as a result technology has passed them by.”
Therein was opportunity for competitors. “The need for email was so acute that customers essentially were betting on a ‘point solution’ for email that might be marginally easier to deploy and manage rather than the complexity of landing what amounts to a development tool on each and every desktop,” recalled Microsoft’s Steven Sinofsky. “We were able to turn the need for email into a need to ride the wave of general-purpose client-server computing, rather than a new category of groupware.” Microsoft would attack the app building side with Microsoft Access, but that was far from the priority. The real fight was over mail — and it was Microsoft Outlook, paired with Exchange Server and its X.500-inspired directory, that won. Standards-compliant email and a rapid embrace of every new feature put universal email at the center of most businesses.
Email would eventually catch up to most of the features Lotus Notes pioneered, rebuilding those features one RFC at a time. It was a glimpse of the future, like Xerox Alto before it. Anyone who used it knew that this was how we’d work in the future. Yet it was too much, when all people really needed was an easier way to communicate.
“The web won because it could evolve faster than Lotus Notes could,” surmised former Iris Associates developer @GMoromisato. “The web won because it was open.” As did email, on the open web—even if it took decades to recreate the future that Lotus Notes showcased in 1989.

results.summary:
Launched in 1989, Lotus Notes pioneered collaborative digital communication and database-driven workflows, offering advanced features like encryption and rich text years before they became standard in modern email.

### Key Points
- Lotus Notes originated from the 1970s PLATO Notes system, which introduced early online forums and synced database communication.
- The platform featured built-in encryption, rich text formatting, file attachments, and cross-platform compatibility long before industry standards like MIME were established.
- Unlike traditional email clients, Lotus Notes functioned as a versatile development environment, allowing users to build custom internal applications, calendars, and forums.
- Its unique, non-standard user interface and complex navigation led to widespread user frustration, famously documented in the "Lotus Notes Interface Hall of Shame."
- Microsoft eventually captured the market by prioritizing standards-compliant email through Outlook and Exchange, which proved more accessible than the complex Lotus Notes ecosystem.

### Why it Matters
Lotus Notes served as a visionary blueprint for modern digital collaboration, demonstrating the power of shared databases and remote connectivity decades before the rise of Slack or Microsoft Teams. While its proprietary nature and steep learning curve ultimately led to its decline, the platform successfully predicted the essential role of integrated, cross-platform communication in the modern workplace.

results.title: Singaporean man pleads guilty in US to massive crypto heist
results.author: Peter Hoskins - Business reporter
results.content:
Singaporean man pleads guilty in US to massive crypto heist
A Singaporean man pleaded guilty on Tuesday to a racketeering conspiracy charge in the US for organising one of the biggest ever cryptocurrency thefts.
Malone Lam admitted to teaming up with friends to steal $245m (£181m) of bitcoin and laundering the proceeds.
The 22-year-old and his associates used the money to spend up to $500,000 per evening at nightclubs, according to the US Department of Justice (DOJ). It also said they bought a fleet of exotic cars, ranging in value from $100,000 to $3.8m.
Lam faces a maximum prison sentence of 20 years. US District Judge Colleen Kollar-Kotelly did not immediately schedule a sentencing hearing for him.
"If you build a cybercrime empire, we will find you, dismantle your operation, and hold you accountable," said US Attorney Jeanine Pirro said.
"This defendant led an international network that preyed on victims through deception, invaded their privacy, and stole hundreds of millions of dollars in cryptocurrency," she added.
Lam told investigators in the US that he had dropped out of secondary school in Singapore when he was 14. He travelled to the US in October 2023 and remained there after his visa expired in January the next year.
According to court documents, the conspiracy began no later than October 2023 and continued to at least May 2025.
The co-conspirators, who came from California, Connecticut, New York, Florida, and outside the US, met via online gaming platforms.
The DOJ said Lam, who also went by the names Anne Hathaway, $$$ and King Greavy, was the ringleader of the criminal enterprise, who identified victims and coordinated the roles of the different conspirators.
They tricked people into giving away confidential information and conducted occasional home break-ins to obtain details that allowed them to drain their victims' cryptocurrency wallets, the DOJ said.
The stolen cryptocurrency was also used to buy Hermes Birkin handbags, valued in the tens of thousands of dollars, which were thrown into crowds at nightclub parties, according to the DOJ.
Other items that the DOJ said the proceeds were spent on included high-end watches worth up to $500,000, luxury clothing valued in the tens of thousands of dollars, rental homes in Los Angeles, the Hamptons, and Miami, private jet rentals for travel and a team of private security guards.
Lam was "notorious" in the Los Angeles and Miami nightclub scenes because of his flamboyant lifestyle, and his crypto windfall had also drawn attention, a Florida district court heard earlier.
His crime ring was dismantled when FBI agents arrested him and a co-conspirator in September 2024.
"As I was listening to the evidence, I could only think of Ferris Bueller gone bad," US magistrate Alicia Valle said during Lam's first court appearance, referring to the 1986 movie about a boy who feigned illness to skip school and go on a wild adventure around Chicago.
"[He] spent this money wildly, going to Los Angeles nightclubs, purchasing more than 30 high-end luxury automobiles. I mean, [that's] an incredible amount of spending and craziness that followed his coming into more than $230 million," the judge said.
In April this year, one of Lam's co-conspirators, Evan Tangeman, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for laundering the proceeds of the scheme.
Tangeman had also tried to destroy evidence after Lam's arrest, which the court took as "consciousness of his guilt", the DOJ said.
results.summary:
Singaporean national Malone Lam pleaded guilty to a racketeering conspiracy charge in a US court for orchestrating a massive cryptocurrency heist that resulted in $245 million in stolen assets.

### Key Points
- Malone Lam admitted to leading an international criminal network that stole $245 million in bitcoin from victims through deception and home break-ins.
- The conspiracy, which operated from October 2023 to May 2025, involved co-conspirators recruited via online gaming platforms.
- Stolen funds were used to finance a lavish lifestyle, including $500,000 nightly nightclub tabs, luxury cars, private jets, and high-end watches.
- Lam faces a maximum sentence of 20 years in federal prison following his arrest by FBI agents in September 2024.
- Co-conspirator Evan Tangeman was previously sentenced to 70 months in prison for his role in laundering the stolen cryptocurrency proceeds.

### Why it Matters
This case highlights the growing sophistication of international cybercrime rings that leverage online gaming communities to coordinate large-scale financial theft. It serves as a significant warning regarding the vulnerability of digital assets and the commitment of federal authorities to dismantle global criminal enterprises.

results.title: SpaceXAI’s Colossus data center is fueling a massive backlash
results.author: Austyn Gaffney
results.content:
Taylor Logsdon was 20 when she and her high school sweetheart moved up their wedding so she could buy a $79,000 house in Colonial Hills, a mixed-income neighborhood of winding, tree-lined streets in Southaven, Miss. At the time, state law would not let her do so alone before she turned 21; she was told marriage would make it possible. About 11 years later that house sits near what could become one of the largest power plants in the state, a thicket of gas turbines assembled to feed SpaceXAI’s artificial-intelligence ambitions.
Beyond Logsdon’s neighborhood, the power plant is mostly hidden. Along the road, black privacy fabric wraps the tall chain-link fence surrounding the Southaven site. Past a thin line of trees, metal stacks rise above the fence, and exhaust shimmers in the heat. A $7-million sound wall does little to muffle the noise, which drills through the walls of nearby homes: a constant drone like a plane taking off and never leaving.
The turbines are there because SpaceXAI needs an enormous amount of electricity for Colossus 2, one of the country’s densest concentrations of computing power, where the company is training Grok, its chatbot. The data center sits just north of the Tennessee state line, in Memphis’s Whitehaven neighborhood; the main power site sits across the border, in Southaven. The gas burns in Mississippi; the electricity crosses to Tennessee. The grid couldn’t deliver enough electricity on SpaceXAI’s timeline, so the company brought generation onsite with portable gas turbines rather than waiting for a conventional power plant or utility upgrade. The turbines were installed under Mississippi’s determination that portable equipment could run for up to a year without air permits. In April the NAACP sued, calling the operation an unpermitted power plant—a fleet that state records later showed had grown to dozens of machines. By July the plant had a capacity of about 1,775 megawatts, rivaling the state’s largest power plants—enough to electrify more than 1.4 million homes or a city more than 60 times Southaven’s size.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Across the country, AI companies are building hyperscale data centers, and power has become the constraint. Data centers now use around 4 to 5 percent of U.S. electricity, and the Electric Power Research Institute projects that share could reach 9 to 17 percent by 2030. “Companies are making a decision that it’s in their best interest to go as fast as possible because every day that they’re not online, they would be losing potential revenue,” says Costa Samaras, an engineering professor and director of the Scott Institute for Energy Innovation at Carnegie Mellon University. Cleanview, an energy-data firm tracking the industry, estimates that AI data centers can generate $10 million to $12 million in annual revenue per megawatt. Bringing a large facility online even a few years early can mean tens of billions of additional dollars.
By June the Southaven dispute had expanded far beyond the city. Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which acquired xAI earlier this year and folded it into an AI arm called SpaceXAI, raised $75 billion in an initial public offering, pushing Musk’s estimated net worth briefly above $1 trillion. A few days later the Department of Justice moved to intervene on xAI’s side and asked the court to dismiss the NAACP suit, arguing that shutting down the power source for Colossus 2 would threaten AI innovation and national security. In a sworn declaration, the Pentagon’s chief digital and artificial-intelligence officer told the court that Grok is one of only four proprietary frontier AI models currently capable of supporting national-security applications. The Pentagon was also a customer: the previous summer it had awarded xAI a contract worth up to $200 million, and the company launched Grok for Government the same day.
In Colonial Hills, the stakes are measured more simply: by who gets the power and who breathes the exhaust.
I met Logsdon in her driveway, where she sat in a deck chair as the brass bell of an ice cream truck occasionally cut through the plant’s drone. Her husband earns $21 an hour as a landscaper. Their mortgage is about $500 a month. She doesn’t believe they could afford to move.
The noise is especially hard on the couple’s kids, all 12 or under, who say it keeps them up at night. Before the turbines arrived, their son, Dallas, was obsessed with xAI’s founder. “We actually were kind of Elon fans,” Logsdon told me. Dallas received a weekly science magazine that featured Musk, and he told his mom he wanted to grow up to be like him. “Elon probably doesn’t know [this plant] was built between two neighborhoods,” she said, “he’s so high up.”
Low-frequency noise from the Southaven turbine plant could be four to 16 times as loud as the background noise typical of a quiet suburban neighborhood, depending on the distance from the plant, according to a March report by acoustics firm Roland, Woolworth & Associates. The noise has drawn its own lawsuit: residents, including Logsdon, filed a class action alleging lost sleep and falling property values.
Logsdon said she is not anti-AI or anti-Musk, but she helped to form the Southaven Safe and Sound Coalition to advocate for her community, especially over the less visible effects of air emissions. She installed three air monitors—two outside her front door and a third atop her camper, the Four Winds Express—to learn what her kids and older neighbors might be breathing. A preliminary analysis of readings taken over four months found that fine-particulate-matter (PM2.5) concentrations around her house exceeded the Environmental Protection Agency’s daily health-protection standard about a third of the time. (The monitors could not determine how much of the pollution came from the power plant.) At least 10 schools, three daycares, two libraries, 11 parks and 27 churches sit within two miles of the plant, according to the coalition.
Dozens of gas turbines in one place can produce very high levels of nitrogen oxides, according to Daniel Cohan, a professor of civil and environmental engineering at Rice University. Those pollutants can irritate the lungs, worsen asthma, and form ground-level ozone, the main ingredient in smog, which builds quickly in the heat of a Mid-South summer.
The NAACP’s lawsuit hinges on whether scores of portable machines operating together constitute a single stationary source, which the plaintiffs argue should trigger the Clean Air Act’s permitting requirements. The Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality, or MDEQ, allowed xAI to operate the turbines without air permits so long as each was removed within 12 months. xAI later received a permit for 41 permanent turbines at the same site, with a total capacity of around 1,200 megawatts. The state’s public hearing on that permit drew more than 300 people, and every speaker opposed it. According to local news reports, no one from the permit board attended, and no one from xAI spoke. At least 27 of those permanent turbines were under construction as of July, according to MDEQ.
In Colonial Hills, the stakes are simpler: who gets the power and who breathes the exhaust.
In January the EPA said temporary turbines that exceed federal emissions thresholds may still require permits. MDEQ had said it would evaluate enforcement if a portable unit remained after the 12-month deadline. On July 30, just before the first units were due to reach that limit, a Mississippi commission acting through MDEQ signed an agreement with xAI affiliate MZX Tech, the SpaceX subsidiary that owns the site, allowing 13 turbines to keep operating through the end of the year, citing delays in construction of the permanent plant. The agreement also set a rolling timetable for the rest of the temporary fleet to be retired as SpaceXAI brings its permitted permanent turbines online.
Portable turbines can be installed quickly, but unlike combined-cycle plants, which can be about 1.5 times as efficient, they do not use their waste heat to generate additional power. “By going with this quick and dirty approach there, [the company] is burning more gas, releasing more pollution and contributing to climate change far more than it needs to be,” Cohan says.
SpaceXAI did not respond to repeated requests for comment.
The strategy had already been tested across the state line. In Memphis, xAI was relying on temporary gas turbines at Colossus 1 by 2024. The site sits in South Memphis, where the surrounding neighborhoods are predominantly Black and ringed by industry that long predates xAI. After public pushback, xAI applied for a permit for 15 permanent turbines in early 2025, but four months later two flyovers by the Southern Environmental Law Center, or SELC, found 35 turbines operating there. After the center threatened to sue, the Shelby County Health Department approved the 15-turbine permit. The dozens of temporary turbines at Colossus 1 disappeared around the same time similar machines began appearing in Mississippi, according to an SELC attorney. In an April letter to the EPA, Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, ranking member of the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works, quoted an xAI senior manager who described the plan as copy and paste from Colossus 1.
In May the NAACP and its Mississippi State Conference sought a preliminary injunction, arguing that 33 unpermitted gas turbines at Southaven could emit 2,508 tons of smog-forming nitrogen oxides every year. A revised motion filed the next month put that scale in local terms, estimating that the site’s emissions could amount to about 26 times those of the TVA Allen gas plant. Abre’ Conner, who leads the NAACP’s environmental and climate justice work, says the organization wanted to make sure other technology companies did not see xAI’s approach as an option.
But the fleet kept growing. In January, xAI said it was running 27 turbines for Colossus 2. MDEQ counted 46 turbines at the Southaven site in May, 60 in June and 69 by July—more than double the number the company had publicly acknowledged at the beginning of the year. Forty-two had been added in 2026, late enough under the agreement’s rolling timetable to remain into 2027; the newest could stay through July of that year.
Before settling on Memphis, xAI reportedly considered eight locations around the country. Musk has said the company was told that building a data center from scratch could take up to two years, so it searched instead for a vacant factory that checked all its boxes. It found one in South Memphis: a former Electrolux plant in an industrial park already threaded with power infrastructure.
The turbines supply warehouse-scale buildings filled with racks of servers built around graphics processing units, or GPUs, the chips first popularized by video games and now prized for training and running AI models. Colossus 1 uses more than 220,000 Nvidia GPUs; Colossus 2 is estimated to use more than twice that amount. Together, Musk has called the facilities the world’s biggest AI supercomputer. Under heavy load, each GPU can draw several hundred watts and generate heat that must be removed. Data centers are increasingly shrink-wrapped around the hardware of their moment; in some cases, building anew can be more efficient than retrofitting for a changeover in chips, cooling systems and power demands.
Colossus is best known for training and running Grok, but the facilities are also becoming a business built on selling computing power. In May, SpaceX disclosed a deal under which Anthropic would pay $1.25 billion a month for capacity across Colossus 1 and Colossus 2, according to the company’s IPO filing. The agreement covers approximately 325,000 GPUs and could total more than $40 billion through May 2029. Grok’s training has moved to Colossus 2, and the company bought an 810,000-square-foot warehouse in Southaven for a third data center, Macrohardrr. In late July, Musk announced another: Minihard in Memphis, with the same GPU capacity as Macrohardrr.
The White House, meanwhile, was pushing AI companies to shoulder their own power needs. In March it rolled out a voluntary Ratepayer Protection Pledge asking AI companies to “build, bring, or buy” the power needed for their data centers and cover related grid-upgrade costs. xAI was one of the signatories. The pledge has no enforcement mechanism, but it encourages the same build-your-own pathway now being challenged in Southaven.
Some Southaven aldermen would talk about SpaceXAI, but several ultimately directed me toward Mayor Darren Musselwhite. He was harder to find. One alderman offered to buy me lunch if I tracked him down. A resident told me the mayor’s nickname was Rapunzel because he was always locked away in his tower. After repeated calls and e-mails and two visits to that tower—Southaven City Hall—Musselwhite did not respond.
A picture began to emerge from my conversations of a project that had become hard for local officials to resist even as trust in SpaceXAI wore thin. Mississippi governor Tate Reeves has called the company’s more than $20-billion Southaven expansion the largest private investment in the state’s history. In a letter included with the DOJ’s court papers, he warned that an injunction could disrupt the state’s economy. Southaven’s mayor said in January that the buildout could bring more than 100 jobs and about $60 million in additional revenue for the city, the county and the school system. The city’s share, he estimated, would exceed $20 billion in 2028—nearly a quarter of its main operating budget. “It’s hard for any community to just say no and turn it down,” alderman-at-large George Payne said on his way to work as an engineer at the local news station. Speaking more broadly about AI, he added, “I’m scared to death of it, as [are] many other people. But I don’t think it’s going to go away. You can’t stop now.”
A few days before the project was revealed, William Jerome, another alderman, signed a nondisclosure agreement—his first—that prevented him from discussing the project publicly before the company announced it. Jerome says the city has nothing to hide, but he would advise other communities to build data centers far from residential areas and to check their local laws before inviting companies in. “I would tell cities to check their zoning because xAI has not done anything illegal,” he says. “For one year they don’t have to get a permit. So are they unpermitted? Yeah, but they’re not illegal.”
Jerome and Payne both say they plan to hold SpaceXAI to its promise to build a quieter, permanent facility to house the turbines. “Now that’s what they [the company] are telling us,” Payne says. “Do I believe with 100 percent certainty? I hope so.”
In Memphis, officials have already been learning the limits of nonbinding promises. At a city council meeting, Sarah Houston, executive director of Protect Our Aquifer, a local water advocacy group, described a recycled-water facility xAI had promised to build. Local officials never secured a binding agreement, and construction paused with the project only partly finished. Houston said completing it would cost another $100 million, less than three days’ worth of payments under Anthropic’s contract for capacity at Colossus 1 and 2.
“We learned at the same time as everyone else” that the project was paused, Doug McGowen, president and CEO of Memphis Light, Gas and Water, told the council. He said xAI had restructured, with an entirely new engineering team in place. SpaceXAI’s president told him and Memphis mayor Paul Young that construction could restart in the first quarter of 2027.
Tannera George Gibson, the city attorney, dismissed Houston’s presentation as “cute” and said the city needed to rely on lawyers, not advocates, for information. Pressed further, Gibson acknowledged that Memphis was leaning on “goodwill and corporate partnership.” Council member Jeff Warren said that the public wanted more accountability. “xAI has had the opportunity to develop these facilities in ways that don’t use water and put water back in cleaner than they take it out, and they haven’t chosen to do it, because they’re in a race against time,” he said.
Local resistance has spread almost as quickly as the data centers themselves. KeShaun Pearson, president of Memphis Community Against Pollution, has spent months traveling through Tennessee, Georgia, Mississippi and Arkansas, trying to turn scattered fights over power and pollution into a Mid-South coalition.
I met him at a barbershop in a strip mall near Memphis’s Frank C. Pidgeon Industrial Center as pink light began to streak the summer sky. He had flown from Atlanta that morning after attending a DeKalb County Board of Commissioners meeting that extended the community’s data center moratorium through September 30.
At least 15 states have considered restrictions or pauses on new data centers, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures, but about half of those proposals have failed. Maine lawmakers passed an 18-month moratorium in spring 2026, but Governor Janet Mills vetoed it. In July, Kathy Hochul, governor of New York State, signed an executive order making hers the first state to impose a statewide pause for new large data centers. Local governments, including DeKalb County, have often been quicker to impose temporary pauses of their own.
Pearson grew up near the industrial park in South Memphis with severe allergies. In a letter opposing the permit for gas turbines at Colossus 1, the Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America warned that the project could add health risks in a region already overburdened with asthma and other respiratory problems. A report published in 2026 showed that Shelby County, which includes Memphis, had received an F from the American Lung Association for its high-ozone days for three years running, from 2022 to 2024. DeSoto County, home to Southaven, also received an F for high-ozone days. Now 37, Pearson said communities like his continue to be treated as “the path of least resistance”—as if their lives do not matter—and “strategically targeted for pollution projects.”
Together we drove toward the industrial park. The unfinished recycled-water facility was marked by two large storage tanks. Across from it sprawled a rail yard and the TVA Allen Combined Cycle Gas Plant, an older answer to the question of who controls power here. Congress created the Tennessee Valley Authority in 1933 to bring electricity and flood control to a struggling region, an experiment in public power that Memphis voted to join the following year. The city became TVA’s largest customer; the relationship has repeatedly frayed over waste, water and power costs. Beyond the plant stood the Nucor steel mill, a cornfield and the Mississippi River.
In the heart of the industrial park sat Colossus 1. “It’s so easy for me to see just how our federal government is being leveraged against us,” Pearson said, referring to the DOJ’s effort to intervene in the Southaven case.
After enormous public pushback against SpaceXAI, Memphis created a community-benefits ordinance. Under it, 25 percent of property-tax revenue from the company’s facilities, up to $100 million, will go toward public-benefit projects in zip codes within a five-mile radius of two of its sites, with 1 percent set aside for environmental work. The ordinance cut against the way Memphis usually courts industry: companies typically negotiate deals that can reduce their property taxes by as much as 75 percent for a set term, but xAI, by Young’s account, asked for no such break. Pearson, however, wants more than money. He wants a moratorium.
In August the Memphis City Council gave initial approval to a temporary pause on new data centers. But for now, the momentum in Southaven is running the other way. The temporary turbines have a negotiated exit schedule, but SpaceXAI has permission to replace them with a permanent power plant. Environmental groups are challenging that permit, and the legal fight over the temporary fleet is still unresolved.
Back in Southaven, Krystal Polk, 52, owns a home close to the fence line, facing the gas plant. Her great-great-grandparents purchased the land, and her parents built the house at a time when few Black families in the area owned property, Polk says. Intruders once wrote “KKK” in the gravel outside the one-story ranch house.
Still, Polk’s family found peace there, watching big owls swoop down and falling asleep to the rustle of two acres of trees. Her three kids grew up spending weekends there while the family lived at another house in town during the workweek. She hosted gatherings there for dozens of relatives. But this year, on the Fourth of July, she canceled a family get-together because the plant was too loud and the prospect of air pollution was too unsettling. “I feel like we are invisible,” she told me from a couch in her living room, her blue dress brushing the floor. “A whole community is saying the same thing, and they’re not listening to them. They have children and babies over there, and elderly, and it’s very heartbreaking.”
Industry is not new to Polk’s family. Warehouses had moved in around the property. Years earlier, TVA representatives visited the house several times to make sure the family knew the utility was building a gas plant nearby and to hear any concerns. Polk said she remembered them as being friendly and respectful.
TVA had come to the door before it began building; xAI never did. Polk said company representatives have instead repeatedly stopped members of her family near the property, asking why they were there or what they were doing—especially when she invited advocates or reporters onto her lawn. “I have to remind them that this is mine,” she said. “I’m not on your property. This is my property.” She and her kids now carry tax records to prove it. “We will be someone’s study eventually,” Polk said. “It’s probably not this year, but as the years go on, we will be the casualties from all of this.”
results.summary:
SpaceXAI is operating a massive, unpermitted fleet of portable gas turbines in Southaven, Mississippi, to power its Colossus 2 data center, sparking legal battles over noise and air pollution.

### Key Points
- SpaceXAI installed dozens of portable gas turbines to power its Grok chatbot, bypassing standard utility upgrades and air permitting requirements.
- The Southaven site’s power capacity has reached 1,775 megawatts, enough to electrify over 1.4 million homes, with emissions potentially exceeding federal health standards.
- The Department of Justice has intervened in a lawsuit against the company, arguing that the facility is critical for national security and AI innovation.
- Residents and the NAACP have filed lawsuits citing constant noise, falling property values, and concerns over fine-particulate-matter pollution near schools and homes.
- Mississippi regulators recently granted an extension allowing 13 temporary turbines to operate through the end of 2026 while permanent infrastructure is under construction.

### Why it Matters
The rapid expansion of AI data centers is creating an urgent conflict between the massive energy demands of tech companies and the health and safety of local communities. This case highlights how the race for computing dominance can lead to the use of "quick and dirty" power solutions that bypass environmental oversight and strain local infrastructure.

results.title: More than 1 in 10 chance AI ‘could kill all humans,’ says Anthropic safety lead after colleague quits
results.author: Robert Hart
results.content:
A senior Anthropic safety researcher has said there is more than a 10 percent chance artificial intelligence “could kill all humans” by the end of the decade, just hours after a colleague resigned over fears the AI lab and its rivals are carelessly racing to build “superhuman systems” they cannot control.
Worried Anthropic researchers warn that AI ‘could kill all humans’
A departing researcher says AI companies are ‘gambling with our lives’ by racing to develop self-improving AI.
In a post on X announcing his departure, Jacob Coxon, a researcher who has trained AI systems at Anthropic, said he had quit the company over its lax approach to safety. Coxon, who previously trained systems for OpenAI, accused the two AI companies of “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” even though “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”
Industry insiders have long expressed concerns about the potential dangers of self-improving AI systems, which they warn could spiral out of human control in a runaway loop often described as recursive self-improvement. While not yet realized, companies are actively pursuing this goal and much of today’s AI code is written with the help of AI.
In a direct response, Evan Hubinger, who leads one of Anthropic’s AI safety teams, said he worries about self-improving AI, adding that it “is happening faster than we thought.” He also agreed with Coxon’s characterization. “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans,” he said, personally estimating the chances to be greater than one in 10 “within the next decade.”
Despite this, Hubinger said Anthropic does “not yet have a plan” for ensuring advanced AI remains safe and aligned with human values and “are not clearly on track to” develop one either. Coxon says the companies are “locked in a race” to develop advanced systems first so are pushing ahead “despite the risk.”
Coxon’s departure marks one of the most high-profile examples of an employee leaving Anthropic, a company founded by former OpenAI members following concerns over safety at the company. In recent years, multiple researchers have cited safety concerns as motivating their decision to leave OpenAI.
The exchange illustrates mounting concerns within the industry about the dangers of increasingly sophisticated AI models and the speed at which systems are being developed, particularly as the companies prepare for anticipated IPOs. It also comes as the companies manage the fallout from numerous rogue agent incidents and high-profile safety warnings about the monitorability of frontier models.
results.summary:
Anthropic safety researcher Evan Hubinger estimates a greater than 10 percent chance that artificial intelligence could cause human extinction within the next decade due to rapid, uncontrolled development.

### Key Points
- Researcher Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic, citing concerns that the company and OpenAI are recklessly racing toward self-improving superintelligence.
- Evan Hubinger, a lead on Anthropic’s safety team, confirmed that the company currently lacks a concrete plan to ensure advanced AI remains aligned with human values.
- Industry experts warn that recursive self-improvement could lead to AI systems spiraling out of human control faster than previously anticipated.
- The departures highlight internal friction at leading AI labs as companies prioritize development speed over safety protocols ahead of potential public offerings.

### Why it Matters
These internal warnings underscore a growing divide between the rapid commercialization of frontier AI models and the industry's ability to guarantee their long-term safety. The lack of established control mechanisms for self-improving systems poses significant regulatory and ethical challenges for the future of the technology sector.

results.title: Sergey Brin is cooking up Google's AI comeback in a California microkitchen
results.author: Hugh Langley
results.content:
Google's AI destiny is being cooked up in a California kitchen.
On the second floor of Gradient Canopy, a tent-like structure that rises east of Google's Mountain View headquarters, is a microkitchen filled with many of the typical fixings: coffee beans, grinders, an espresso machine, a fridge. Less typical is the U-shaped formation of desks, used by Google cofounder Sergey Brin and a handful of mission-critical leaders who are steering Google through an AI race it can't afford to lose.
Google CEO Sundar Pichai visits the break-turned-war-room several times a week. Employees from other parts of the building sometimes saunter in for an extended snack break, hoping to overhear gossip that could reveal Google's next big move. There are whispers that cofounder Larry Page has been spotted there.
This unlikely nerve center has gained more influence in the weeks since Google shook up its AI leadership.
Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis, who was helping steer the company's AI efforts from London, relinquished his title and became Alphabet's chief scientist. Koray Kavukcuoglu, who moved from London to the US last year and now sits alongside Brin in the microkitchen, was appointed SVP of Google DeepMind, effectively replacing Hassabis. Jeff Dean, Google's longtime chief scientist, left the company after 27 years.
Brin's role in the new power structure went unmentioned.
However, the man who helped launch Google from a garage nearly three decades ago has become increasingly influential over Gemini, eight current and former employees told Business Insider, in part thanks to his unique ability to pull resources for critical work and cut through the tech giant's bureaucracy. The latest changes at the top, some of them said, could give Brin even more sway over Gemini.
It's a role seen by some inside Google as necessary after the 2023 merger of the company's two central AI labs led to friction over the direction of Gemini that slowed progress and prompted a stream of departures. Some of Mountain View's leaders became frustrated with Hassabis and other researchers in London, believing they weren't as pragmatic about making Gemini more competitive to rivals, two people familiar with the matter said.
Up against the corporate machinery of Google, the microkitchen has acted as something of a startup inside the larger company, allowing Brin, Kavukcuoglu, and other leaders to make decisions faster. "The promise of the kitchen is that it can help you cut through the politics," said one former employee familiar with the setup.
Such decisions are more crucial than ever. Google has fallen behind the frontier, which is putting more pressure on it to make its next model, Gemini 4, a blockbuster event. The company has lost top talent in recent months, including star computer scientists John Jumper and Noam Shazeer. Against this backdrop, Brin has urged employees to double their efforts on Gemini.
"Demis is obviously very talented, but he's moving farther away, not closer, to the operational part. This glimmer of hope is this notion that Sergey will get more involved," said Gil Luria, head of technology research at the investment bank D.A. Davidson. "They need a big change that will cut through that bureaucracy."
Google declined to comment on this story, and declined to make Brin and other leaders available for interviews.
Letting Brin cook
Brin's position is highly unusual.
He no longer holds an executive title at Google, yet he and Page have decisive influence over the company's board due to a special controlling stock.
After he and Page stepped back from running Alphabet in 2019, Brin spent his time building airships, partying at Burning Man, and writing about physics. When ChatGPT launched in late 2022, and Google was suddenly playing catch-up, Brin said the temptation to return to the trenches was just too much. "As a computer scientist I've never seen anything as exciting as all of the AI progress that's happened in the last few years," he said during the All-In Summit in Los Angeles in 2024.
Brin's unique perch inside Google makes him a powerful ally for any Googler who wants to accrue more support for their project or idea. Getting access to Google's chips, even for the Gemini team, can be difficult. The official route is to submit a formal document and get buy-in from higher-ups. Another route is to strike a deal with a different team inside Google to use their chips in exchange for, say, building Gemini features for their products, two people familiar with such arrangements said.
The other, less official route is to go to Brin.
"Koray has more explicit power in the hierarchy, but Sergey is the founder of Google," said a former senior employee. "He's able to cut through bureaucracy and clear red tape in a way no one else can." People who have worked at Google DeepMind said Kavukcuoglu and Brin have a good rapport, and that when Brin wants something done, he will often do it through Kavukcuoglu. However, Brin usually gets his way, three people said.
Over the past two years, the microkitchen's gravitational pull has grown stronger. Kavukcuoglu moved from London to Mountain View last year and now sits close to Brin. Sebastian Borgeaud, a research engineer, also moved across the Atlantic last year and was appointed to lead work on improving Gemini's coding abilities, two people familiar with the move said. A huddle of desks was set up for the coding strike team inside the microkitchen, close to Brin and Kavukcuoglu, a person familiar with the matter said.
"Sergey wants to run Gemini like a startup," said a former employee with direct knowledge of the arrangement. "If you want to be part of the startup, you have to be in the microkitchen."
Emanuel Taropa, a Google fellow and a legendary name in the AI research community, often sits in the kitchen, two people said. So does Enrique Piqueras, a senior research engineer on Gemini, who insiders described as an especially close ally of Brin's. Another oft-spotted face in the kitchen is Rahul Arya, a physics Olympiad who has played a central role in improving Google's AI chips. Insiders say that Google has made a concerted effort not to publicize some of its most important stars for fear of them being poached.
If you can't handle the heat
Brin has largely involved himself in the technical aspects of Gemini, weighing in on discussions about model sizes, release windows, and paths to artificial general intelligence, according to current and former employees. He also got involved in some internal disagreements last year over how Gemini should be integrated into Google products, two people said.
One idea Brin pushed earlier this year was to use software to monitor some Google employees as they coded, believing it could be a useful reinforcement learning technique to improve Gemini's coding abilities, a person familiar with the project said.
At times, Brin has made calls that have frustrated some staff. In 2025, Dean, Google's now-former chief scientist, was leading efforts to build a chip that would embed a version of the Gemini model architecture directly onto the silicon, a project internally codenamed Frozen. The project was unpopular among some Gemini leaders, two former employees said. Brin made the call to cut the project — a decision that frustrated Dean, who told some colleagues around that time he was considering leaving the company, said one of the people who heard the remarks.
The project was later revived as Frozen v2; however, some of its resources were stripped away from it earlier this year, the person added. Dean left Google in August to launch his own startup. He declined to comment on this story.
Some employees bristled at a post Brin made in an internal Google DeepMind work channel in 2025, stating that working about 60 hours a week is the "sweet spot" for productivity, which was first reported by The New York Times. One former manager said that they told their employees to ignore Brin's memo.
Earlier this year, during a Q&A session at San Francisco's AGI House, Brin was asked how he was splitting his responsibilities with Kavukcuoglu and Hassabis. Brin said he worked closely with Kavukcuoglu and would often "poke and prod" the teams when he was unhappy with their direction, describing himself as "sometimes a little bit disruptive."
"I'll be honest, I'm a little bit of a rabble-rouser," he said.
Brain trust
When Google announced in 2023 that it would combine DeepMind with its core Brain AI team, it capped a near-decade journey for Hassabis. Since selling DeepMind to Google in 2014, the Nobel laureate had fought to keep his lab independent, determined to pursue research free of Google's bureaucracy and untethered from products he considered irrelevant to his north star: building artificial general intelligence.
The 2023 merger was evidence to some inside DeepMind that any hopes of exercising independence under Google were misplaced. It was also around this time that Brin began showing up to work on Gemini. While Google said nothing publicly about Brin's return, there were clues. A March 2023 post on LinkedIn showed Luxembourg Deputy Prime Minister Xavier Bettel meeting Pichai, Google's global affairs president Kent Walker, and — wearing sweatpants — Brin.
Google was in wartime mode, but there was also a battle brewing within. Brain and DeepMind had different cultures, three people who worked there at the time said. Brain typically worked more closely on improving Google's products, and teams in DeepMind had focused more on longer-term research that often didn't have near-term commercial viability. "There was tension in the DNA of what DeepMind wanted to be," said a former employee. "Do they want to be a 10-year research bet working on things that make humanity incredible, or are they going to win this 3-6 month horizon race between the labs?"
In 2023, Kavukcuoglu chose to build Gemini using some of the people and infrastructure behind Chinchilla, a prior language model developed by the London DeepMind team, rather than on Google's PaLM 2. The decision was unpopular with some researchers in Mountain View, who saw it as favoritism toward the London group, two people said.
After Brin returned to the trenches in 2023, he began working in the microkitchen. Taropa, the Google fellow, was also a core founding member of the kitchen office. Over time, more desks were added, and the space became the de facto command center, often referred to by staff as "Sergey's microkitchen." At one point, an overflow space was added because many employees wanted to be closer to what had quickly become the power center of Gemini.
'AGI-pilled'
Brin has spent less time in the kitchen in recent months, sometimes showing up on alternating weeks, according to two people who have seen him there. Ahead of a possible new billionaire's tax, the Google cofounder moved some of his personal assets out of California last December and purchased homes in Florida and Nevada.
The measure, if it passes on a November ballot, would impose a one-time tax on California residents with a net worth exceeding $1 billion. Brin, who has mounted a large-scale opposition effort against the tax, could be liable to pay $14 billion if he were considered a resident.
Ahead of the recent leadership shuffle, Brin appeared frustrated with the pace at which Google is moving on Gemini and has pushed employees for more focus on recursive self-improvement (RSI), the point where systems can improve themselves, current and former employees said. "He's very invested in RSI. He's very AGI-pilled," said one former employee. Reuters previously reported on some of Brin's remarks around RSI.
Insiders described the August reorg as a win for the more technical side of the company and the further erosion of DeepMind's independence, underscoring the commercial reality of the AI race. In recent weeks, the company has shown signs of positive progress. It recently rehired Barret Zoph, the Thinking Machines Labs cofounder, in what some insiders said could be a big win for Google. The company has said its latest Gemini model shows "significant" improvements in coding.
Will it be enough? Google is still bleeding talent. The AI coding software market has fast become crowded, which could make it harder for Google to break in meaningfully, said Luria, the analyst. What Google needs, he said, is a major breakthrough that will vault its models to the state of the art. "Short of that, everything is tactical, and they'll continue to need to catch up," he said.
The September release of ChatGPT's Astra model appears to have pushed the frontier forward again, and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has suggested even smarter models are waiting in the wings.
Google needs momentum, and with Brin more involved than ever, some employees are hopeful it will find it. From a garage to a kitchen, Google's most consequential work has a habit of happening in unlikely rooms.
Have something to share? Contact this reporter via email at hlangley@businessinsider.com or Signal at 628-228-1836.
results.summary:
Google cofounder Sergey Brin has established an influential "microkitchen" command center at the company's Mountain View headquarters to accelerate the development of the Gemini artificial intelligence model.

### Key Points
- Sergey Brin is actively steering Gemini development by bypassing corporate bureaucracy and directly managing key technical resources and personnel.
- Koray Kavukcuoglu has been appointed SVP of Google DeepMind, working closely with Brin to align AI research with product-focused goals.
- The "microkitchen" serves as a startup-like hub where Brin and his team make rapid decisions on model architecture, release windows, and resource allocation.
- Recent leadership changes include Demis Hassabis transitioning to Alphabet’s chief scientist and the departure of longtime chief scientist Jeff Dean.
- Google is under significant pressure to improve Gemini’s performance to remain competitive against rivals like OpenAI in the rapidly evolving AI market.

### Why it Matters
This shift toward a founder-led, agile command structure highlights Google's urgent attempt to regain its competitive edge in the high-stakes artificial intelligence race. By centralizing power around Brin, the company aims to overcome internal friction and bureaucratic delays that have hindered its ability to match the rapid innovation of industry peers.

results.title: Apple Event Live Blog: Folding iPhone, Apple Watch Series 12, AirPods, and More
results.author: WIRED
results.content:
Welcome to our live coverage of today's Apple media showcase. Our reporters on the scene at Apple Park in Cupertino, California, to bring you live coverage. You'll be hearing from Julian Chokkattu, Boutayna Chokrane, Lauren Goode, Reece Rogers, and Michael Calore throughout the event.
More About How the Apple Watch Listens to You
The new Apple Watches include several “intelligent” listening features that have privacy and security baked in. But the protections can’t change the facts of what the tools do.
Read the full story about the new listening features on WIRED.
OK, so, the Duo starts at $1999. That's eye-watering, but not surprising. This is a theme across Apple's product line now, as Julian noted: Some products, like iPad and MacBook, are just more expensive.
That's partly because of bill of materials (memory), partly because Apple has not actually diversified its cash flow all that much over the past decade or so aside from growing its services business (which generates a lot of gross profit). But even as some product shipments decline—depending on which quarter you're looking at—Apple needs to maintain its margins.
Everything about the Duo is bigger, faster, longer thank other iPhones. Which is normal for Apple when it’s telling you about its new products; everything is the best version yet!
But it feels like going to a dual screen lets Apple take a significantly bigger step forward. The battery, the screen, the chips—there’s more room for all of it, and the company is really able to flex its technical muscle here.
results.summary:
Apple unveiled its latest product lineup at a Cupertino media event, highlighted by the introduction of the new Duo smartphone and advanced intelligent listening features for Apple Watches.

### Key Points
- Apple hosted a media showcase at its headquarters in Cupertino, California, to debut new hardware and software features.
- The new Duo smartphone features a dual-screen design, improved battery life, and faster processing chips.
- New Apple Watch models include integrated intelligent listening tools designed with specific privacy and security protocols.
- Pricing for the new Duo starts at $1,999, reflecting a broader trend of rising costs across Apple’s MacBook and iPad product lines.
- Apple is prioritizing high profit margins and its growing services business to offset fluctuations in global product shipment volumes.

### Why it Matters
The introduction of the high-priced Duo signals Apple's strategy to maintain profitability by leveraging premium hardware designs and expanded service offerings. This shift highlights the company's ongoing effort to balance technical innovation with the financial necessity of sustaining margins amid shifting consumer demand.

results.title: The Coolest Thing I Saw at IFA 2026: The Coolest, Quietest, Thinnest Laptop Concept
results.author: Matt Elliott
results.content:
Some concepts on display at trade shows are simply bald attempts at garnering attention on a noisy and crowded show floor. And then there are others that provide actual glimpses into the future. Lenovo’s Project Aero falls into the latter category. (I’d put all of its rollable display concepts into the former: fun to see in action, but not something I’d look for in my next purchase.)
There wasn’t much to the ThinkBook laptop used for Lenovo’s Project AeroBlade concept that would get you to stop and take notice. Other than being thinner and lighter than the typical laptop, it looked like a run-of-the-mill business ultraportable. And the Project AeroBlade demo wasn’t particularly compelling on the surface. The laptop’s screen didn’t magically expand at the press of a button to draw oohs and aahs. But under the hood, there was some tech that I hope moves from concept to reality before I need to buy my next laptop.
Active cooling without fans (and their noise)
The concept of Project AeroBlade is moving air in and out of the ThinkBook without the use of any traditional cooling fans. Lenovo calls it Active Flow, a solid-state active cooling system. Instead of fans, Active Flow uses small AirJet modules from Frore Systems. We’ve seen Frore’s AirJet modules before, but this is the first time we’ve seen them in an actual laptop.
AirJet modules use ultrasonic vibrations to pull cool air into the laptop and expel hot air out of it. These tiny modules are about the size of a mobile processor and are just 2.7 millimeters thick, and yet they are incredibly powerful. According to a Frore representative, an AirJet creates 10 times the back pressure, or suction, of a traditional laptop cooling fan.
With four AirJet modules inside instead of a pair of cooling fans, the ThinkBook that Lenovo used for its Project AeroBlade was impossibly thin and light. It was a 14-inch laptop that was only 11mm thick, or about 0.4 inches thick, and weighed just 1.8 pounds. When I picked it up, it felt like a movie prop — an empty shell of a laptop rather than an actual operating machine.
In addition to being very compact, the laptop looked extra polished with a bottom panel that was solid and smooth. Because the AirJets are more effective at moving air in and out of the laptop, the ThinkBook could be designed without any bottom intake vents. All of the air is pulled in and pushed out of a thin vent along the laptop’s back edge.
Powerful and portable
The promise of Project AeroBlade is getting higher-powered CPUs in thinner and lighter designs. With fanless laptops, you must sacrifice some performance in the form of a low-voltage or throttled processor for the thinness and lightness.
The ThinkBook on display was running a mainstream Core Ultra 7 Lunar Lake 17-watt chip. I wonder if it’ll be able to accommodate a 25-watt Panther Lake or just a lower-wattage WildCat Lake that’s closer in thermal design power to Lunar Lake. And with the laptops we’ll soon see with Nvidia’s RTX Spark, can we look forward to a combination of a 38-watt RTX Spark and AirJet active cooling in the near future?
Read more: Lenovo’s Latest Laptop Gives Off MacBook Neo Vibes
Another AirJet benefit is acoustics. Like a fanless laptop, the ThinkBook operates in silence but with active cooling that moves air in and out. I could not hear or feel the AirJet modules’ vibrations as they worked.
Further, without any moving parts, the laptop should last longer. Traditional cooling fans get gummed up with dirt and dust and, with their moving parts, are a common point of failure. I’d equate it to solid-state drives generally lasting longer than hard drives with spinning platters.
Lenovo wouldn’t comment on when this concept might turn into a final shipping laptop. And Frore didn’t say if it was working with other laptop manufacturers in addition to Lenovo. But given how much thinner and smaller the AirJet modules are in comparison to cooling fans, plus the fact that they can be located in different areas of the motherboard where heat dissipation is needed the most, implementing them will require a rethinking and reworking of laptop motherboard architecture. This reengineering will require some time, but I’m hoping we will see Lenovo release an AirJet-cooled ThinkBook next year. I also hope Frore’s AirJet tech will spread to other laptops beyond Lenovo’s.
I can envision a not-so-distant future where cooling fans inside laptops become as antiquated as traditional spinning hard drives.
results.summary:
Lenovo’s Project AeroBlade concept introduces a fanless cooling system using Frore Systems’ AirJet modules, enabling significantly thinner, lighter, and quieter laptop designs without sacrificing high-performance processor capabilities.

### Key Points
- Lenovo’s Project AeroBlade utilizes Active Flow technology, replacing traditional mechanical cooling fans with solid-state AirJet modules from Frore Systems.
- The AirJet modules use ultrasonic vibrations to generate high back pressure, measuring only 2.7 millimeters in thickness.
- The prototype ThinkBook measures just 11mm thick and weighs 1.8 pounds, featuring a solid bottom panel without traditional intake vents.
- The system successfully cooled a 17-watt Intel Core Ultra 7 Lunar Lake processor while operating in complete silence.
- Eliminating moving parts like fans reduces potential hardware failure points and prevents dust accumulation inside the laptop chassis.

### Why it Matters
This technology could fundamentally change laptop architecture by allowing manufacturers to pack high-performance processors into ultra-thin chassis that were previously limited by thermal constraints. If adopted widely, solid-state cooling may eventually render mechanical fans obsolete, leading to more durable and silent computing devices.

results.title: Steam achievements for unreleased and unannounced games leak on aggregators such as Exophase and SteamDB
results.author: Sophie McEvoy
results.content:
Achievements for unreleased and unannounced games on Steam have been leaked, including Fable, Persona 6, Kingdom Hearts 4, and Control Resonant.
According to GameDiscoverCo founder Simon Carless, Valve "unfortunately rolled out a major bug around achievements" after its "weekly maintenance window."
"As a result, automated data collectors of Steam achievement info such as Exophase and SteamDB are collecting achievement data for every single Steam game that has one, even those unreleased... or even unannounced," said Carless.
Exophase owner Mike Bendel stated this was an error by Valve, not a data leak. Replying to a user on ResetEra, Bendel said "a bunch of games with achievements that should be private are accessible through API right now and that's why they got scanned into the site."
"I usually never see games without an actual name pop up with achievements, yet over the past hour or so a bunch have (when there's an unknown name we just set it to the AppID)."
Per Gematsu, other games affected include Gears of War: E-Day, Clutch, Horizon Hunters Gathering, Ace Combat 8, Metro 2039, Star Wars: Galactic Racer, Stranger Than Heaven, Rayman Legends: Retold, and Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis.
GamesIndustry.biz has contacted Valve for further information.
In July, Valve confirmed that European customers' data was compromised following a breach at Valve's regional shipping partner for Steam hardware, CEVA Logistics.
Valve told GamesIndustry.biz the attack on CEVA occurred between July 29 and August 1, and that it learned of the breach on August 7.
results.summary:
A technical error in Valve’s Steam maintenance window has exposed achievement data for numerous unannounced and unreleased video games, including titles from major franchises like Fable and Persona.

### Key Points
- A bug in Valve’s Steam API allowed third-party tracking sites like SteamDB and Exophase to scrape achievement data for private, unreleased game projects.
- Affected titles include Kingdom Hearts 4, Gears of War: E-Day, Control Resonant, and several other high-profile upcoming releases.
- Exophase owner Mike Bendel confirmed the incident was a platform-side technical error rather than a traditional data breach or malicious hack.
- The leak occurred following a routine weekly maintenance window, causing automated collectors to pull information that should have remained hidden.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights the vulnerability of pre-release game metadata when platform APIs fail to enforce privacy settings correctly. The exposure of these titles provides an unprecedented look at upcoming industry projects, potentially disrupting marketing plans and official reveal schedules for major publishers.
