results.title: Citing the 'Deep State,' Trump overhauls the intelligence community
results.author: Greg Myre
results.content:
Citing the 'Deep State,' Trump overhauls the intelligence community
John Sipher spent nearly three decades at the CIA focused on the Russians, a core part of the agency's mission. That changed dramatically after the al-Qaida attacks on Sept. 11, 2001.
"Frankly, tracking and hunting terrorists, finding people, finding a needle in a haystack was not something that we trained for," said Sipher, who served in Moscow and later ran the agency's Russia operations at CIA headquarters.
The CIA and the larger intelligence community had to adapt quickly.
"We did that by by learning, and actually even developing new technologies, computer power, data collection, drones, communications, means to defeat networks, terrorist networks," he said.
There were real successes, such as locating Osama bin Laden in 2011 and destroying his group, al-Qaida, and later, dismantling the Islamic State.
More broadly, the Department of Homeland Security was created, and now has a quarter-million employees, making it the second-largest government agency, trailing only the Pentagon. Military and intelligence budgets soared.
By most all accounts, the U.S. is safer at home. The country has not been hit on U.S. soil with anything remotely comparable to the 9/11 attack, which killed nearly 3,000 people.
Trump targets the "deep state"
Yet 25 years later, U.S. national security industry is undergoing another dramatic change.
President Trump is waging an ongoing campaign against the so-called "deep state," which he describes largely as national security officials trying to undermine him.
"We will clean out all of the corrupt actors in our national security and intelligence apparatus, and there are plenty of them," Trump said in announcing his plans for his second term.
Critics say Trump is tearing down the national security infrastructure with no clear vision of what comes next, aside from protecting the president's personal interests.
"Since the re-inauguration of Donald Trump, the architecture of American national security is being destroyed, just like the east wing of the White House," said author Tim Weiner, who's covered the U.S. intelligence community for decades. This includes a book last year, The Mission: The CIA in the 21st Century, that examines the CIA since 9/11. "Trump has deliberately swung a wrecking ball through American national security and has in great part worked to dismantle the systems set up after World War II to protect the United States.
Weiner said Trump consistently selects loyalists with limited experience to lead national security agencies.
"The people he has put in charge, [Pete] Hegseth at the Pentagon, Kash Patel at the FBI, John Ratcliffe at CIA, are sycophants," said Weiner. "They will tell the president what he wants to know rather than what he needs to know."
Cutbacks at home, strained relations abroad
While many officials have been dismissed under Trump, some left on their own.
Steven Cash held multiple national security posts — at the CIA, the Senate Intelligence Committee and the Department of Homeland Security.
He resigned when Trump began his second term.
"I could not in good conscience keep working for a president who was going to take what I was working on and what others had spent careers working on, and turning it against Americans, which is exactly what he has done," Cash said.
Cash now leads the Steady State, a private group of more than 400 former national security officials. They were career officials who served in both Republican and Democratic administrations, but are now highly critical of Trump's policies.
Cash believes the intelligence community made important advances over the past quarter-century, particularly in information sharing. But he acknowledges it's been an imperfect process.
The post of director of national intelligence, or DNI, was created to coordinate the work of what are now 18 separate intelligence agencies.
"The original idea was it would be very small," Cash said. "We sort of joked that the new DNI would get a deputy, he'd get a big conference table with 18 chairs, and the biggest, best coffee machine he could find. And other than that, he'd get nothing."
The office quickly swelled and is often criticized for not functioning as intended. There are periodic calls for the office to be abolished.
Trump cut back the office, along with other national security agencies, as part of his larger government reductions.
Cash said these moves have gone way too far.
"We took a dive off the cliff in 2025. All the gains, I think, are gone, and we are in the process of destroying our intelligence community," he said.
Shifting agendas
U.S. successes in fighting terrorism have made it less of a priority these days, leading to cutbacks, according to Marc Polymeropoulos, a former CIA officer who spent much of his career in the Middle East.
"Counterterrorism is getting second fiddle to the threats from China and Russia, and the current administration's focus on the border and narco-trafficking means a shift of resources to the Americas," said Polymeropoulos. "I am afraid that counter-terrorism will not be a priority until a mass casualty event, and then it very much will be once again."
John Sipher says one of the most damaging ideas that's taken root is that career intelligence officials actively take sides in partisan politics.
"We have allowed our partisan anger, and specifically the Trump administration, to create this narrative that there's a deep state and that the intelligence services work for one party or another. I think it's a real danger," he said.
Tim Weiner said the damage has also been inflicted abroad as Trump repeatedly antagonizes U.S. allies.
"The CIA in particular relies or depends on intelligence sharing with friendly and not so friendly foreign intelligence services," Weiner said. "It it is still only 20,000 people, and they cannot cover the entire world. They need the British. They need the Dutch. They need the Saudis. They need help."
That help, he says, is much harder to come by today than in the aftermath of 9/11.
results.summary:
President Trump is actively restructuring the U.S. intelligence community and national security apparatus, citing a need to eliminate a "deep state" of corrupt actors within federal agencies.

### Key Points
- President Trump has appointed loyalists, including Pete Hegseth at the Pentagon, Kash Patel at the FBI, and John Ratcliffe at the CIA, to lead national security agencies.
- The administration is implementing significant budget and personnel reductions across intelligence departments, including the Office of the Director of National Intelligence.
- Former officials, such as Steven Cash, argue these changes dismantle decades of progress in information sharing and institutional stability established after 9/11.
- Strategic priorities are shifting away from counterterrorism toward competition with China and Russia, as well as increased focus on border security and narco-trafficking.
- Critics warn that antagonizing foreign allies and replacing career experts with political loyalists undermines the intelligence sharing necessary for global security operations.

### Why it Matters
These structural changes represent a fundamental shift in how the United States manages its national security and intelligence gathering capabilities. The move risks long-term institutional instability and could weaken critical international partnerships that rely on consistent, non-partisan intelligence cooperation.

results.title: The Death Of The Button: Why The Best Interface Is No Interface
results.author: hello@smashingmagazine.com (Carrie Webster)
results.content:
Ever since the commercialisation of the Graphical User Interface pioneered by systems like the Xerox Star and popularised by the original Apple Macintosh, software has relied heavily on point-and-click interactions. If you wanted to book a trip, buy a pair of shoes, or research a health symptom, you were expected to navigate a labyrinth of user interfaces. You click menus, adjust range sliders, fill out multi-step forms, deal with cookie pop-ups, and open dozens of browser tabs just to cross-reference basic information. We have become accustomed to spending more time managing the software rather than actually achieving our goals.
That contract is officially changing. Driven by advances in artificial intelligence and large language models, a new generation of web tools is pioneering a radical philosophy: Intent-Driven Design. Rather than expecting our users to learn complex menus and click through elaborate sales funnels, these platforms operate by capturing high-level human goals and silently executing the grunt work in the background.
This vision builds on long-standing HCI concepts like Golden Krishna’s “The Best Interface Is No Interface” and Don Norman’s principles of human-centered design.
“
Well, at least what we understand based on our current experience.
It is essential for UX designers to understand the changes we’re witnessing and even re-evaluate our role, shifting our focus from designing visible interfaces to guiding transparent, intent-driven AI experiences.
The Death Of The “10-click” Process
To understand where web design is going, we first have to look at the friction we have accepted as “normal” for decades.
Consider the traditional workflow of buying a flight online. The user experience is intentionally hyper-interactive:
- Navigate to a travel aggregator or airline website.
- Select “Round Trip” from a dropdown menu.
- Type the origin city and wait for auto-complete.
- Type the destination city and wait for auto-complete.
- Click a calendar modal, toggle through months, and select departure and return dates.
- Choose the number of passengers and cabin class.
- Click “Search” and wait for the results page to load.
- Filter by price, layover duration, departure time, and airline.
- Sort the results and scan through dozens of individual options.
- Click through a three-page checkout funnel dodging upsells for rental cars and travel insurance.
This is a classic point-and-click UI paradigm. The computer acts as a passive container of data, and the human acts as the orchestrator, manually inputting parameters, interpreting raw outputs, and executing each micro-step along the way.
Intent-driven design flips this dynamic entirely. Instead of forcing you to navigate the mechanical steps of how to find a flight, the interface asks a simple question: What are you trying to accomplish?
When you express a goal, such as “Find me a non-stop flight to Chicago next weekend under $300 that arrives before 5 PM”, the software reads your intent, executes the multi-step search query behind the scenes, compares the options, and presents a single actionable resolution. The ten clicks dissolve into one clear intent outcome.
Three Web Platform Examples Replacing Buttons With Intent
This shift isn’t a theoretical vision of the distant future. Some of the world’s most accessible websites allow you to experience intent-capturing systems already.
1. Perplexity AI: Search Without The Open Tabs
Traditional search engines like Google were built as directories. You typed a keyword, and the interface rewarded you with ten blue links. The actual work of opening five tabs, skimming long articles, dodging ads, and manually assembling an answer was left to you. Although this is now changing, with AI content appearing first when you search on Google.
Perplexity AI allows anyone to perform instant intent-based searches. Instead of forcing you to click into multiple tabs, the interface synthesises the perfect result for your context.
- The interaction: You ask a complex question in plain English: “Compare the top three budget laptops for a computer science student, focusing on battery life and keyboard quality.”
- The invisible work: In under two seconds, the platform searches the web, reads dozens of articles, evaluates hardware specifications, and cross-references user reviews.
- The result: (See screen above) Instead of throwing web pages at you, Perplexity dynamically generates a single custom answer complete with formatted comparison tables, pros and cons lists, and concise inline citations. You get the outcome of thirty clicks in just one.
2. Vercel v0: Web Design Without Dragging And Dropping
For years, creating a website meant using visual builders like Figma or drag-and-drop web editors. As designers, we spent hours manually drawing rectangles, picking hexadecimal colour codes, adjusting padding values, and sometimes writing CSS code.
Vercel v0 lets anyone test its generative interface builder right from the home page without signing in.
- The Interaction: A user types a descriptive goal into the input prompt: “Create a modern dark-mode dashboard for a subscription SaaS app showing monthly revenue, active users, and a customer churn chart.”
- The invisible work: The underlying AI understands layout principles, accessibility guidelines, UI component libraries, and responsiveness. It writes clean HTML, Tailwind CSS, and React code in real time.
- The result: Rather than spending an afternoon manipulating elements, the user receives a fully functional, pixel-perfect user interface in seconds! The traditional visual design tool disappears, replaced by raw human intent.
3. Goblin.tools: Breaking Down Overwhelming Tasks
Many traditional productivity tools require you to manually construct task lists, drag items across Kanban boards, and assign micro-deadlines. Goblin.tools is a free, single-page suite of single-task AI tools designed specifically for neurodivergent users or anyone feeling overwhelmed, requiring zero sign-ups or configuration.
- The interaction: You enter a vague, intimidating goal into the Magic Todo tool, such as “Prepare for a job interview”.
- The invisible work: Instead of forcing you to plan every step, the system analyses the cognitive load of the goal and automatically breaks it down into small, actionable sub-tasks adjusted to your preferred level of detail.
- The result: The interface eliminates the stressful task-planning phase and presents a clean checklist tailored to your exact goal.
The Core Pillars Of Intent-driven Web Design
When you remove traditional menus, sidebars, and forms, how do you keep a website usable? Designers pioneering this space rely on three core pillars:
| Pillar | Traditional UX approach | Intent-driven UX approach | 
|---|---|---|
| User input | Micro-actions (Clicks, dropdowns, toggles) | 1. High-level goals (Natural language, context, habits) | 
| Interface state | Static layouts (Everyone sees the same page) | 2. Generative UI (Layouts created dynamically on the fly) | 
| Task execution | Manual execution by the user | 3. Autonomous execution by background AI agents | 
1. High-level Goals
An invisible interface doesn’t always wait for you to type a command — it leverages context to anticipate user needs. Guided by industry standards like Apple’s Human Interface Guidelines on Contextual & Ambient Design, modern systems read environmental metadata, such as device state, location, and past interaction patterns, to trigger proactive actions.
For example:
- Time and location: A food delivery web app prioritising your saved home address and dinner items automatically at 6:30 PM on a weekday.
- Cross-app history: A calendar application noticing an email about an upcoming appointment and surfacing a one-click “Add to Schedule” card without forcing you to copy and paste event details manually.
2. Generative UI
In traditional web design, every user sees the exact same layout. An e-commerce store shows the same navigation bar whether you are a first-time visitor looking for customer support or a returning customer tracking a package.
As highlighted in the Nielsen Norman Group’s analysis on AI as a new UX paradigm, computing is shifting from command-based interaction to outcome-specification. This enables Generative UI, where interfaces are rendered dynamically on the fly based on what you are trying to do in that exact moment. For example, platforms like Vercel v0 demonstrate how raw intent can instantly render functional code components without manual layout building. If you express a desire to compute complex financial data, the interface generates a dynamic calculator widget on demand, receding once your goal is completed.
3. Execution by AI Agents
Traditional interfaces are obsessed with prevention, constantly peppering users with confirmation pop-ups (“Are you sure you want to delete this file?”).
Intent-driven interfaces adapt Jakob Nielsen’s 10 Usability Heuristics on User Control and Error Recovery by shifting the safety net from prevention to easy reversibility. Because autonomous agents take actions on your behalf, products prioritise frictionless rollback mechanisms. A prominent “Undo” button, simple revision prompts (“Make this summary shorter”), and transparent audit logs replace intrusive warning modals.
The Hidden Risks
While removing interface friction is liberating, stripping away visual controls introduces significant product design challenges. When software acts on inferred intent rather than direct point-and-click commands, designers must navigate critical ethical and technical pitfalls.
The Illusion Of Control
When a website makes decisions for you, it can quickly feel patronising or invasive. As explored by the Stanford Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) Group, automation must maintain clear boundaries to prevent user frustration. Furthermore, ethical frameworks from the Center for Humane Technology emphasise that product designers must guard against manipulative defaults.
Designers must strike a delicate balance: automate routine execution, but explicitly prompt the user for high-stakes confirmations (such as financial transactions, publishing public content, or altering privacy settings).
The Black Box Problem
In a traditional UI, if you get an unexpected result, you can usually diagnose the issue — perhaps you checked the wrong filter box or selected an incorrect date.
With an intent-driven interface, troubleshooting becomes harder. To address this “black box” challenge, the Google PAIR (People + AI Research) Guidebook advocates for transparent feedback loops. The system must explicitly state its interpretation (“Searching for non-stop flights to Chicago under $300…”) so users can calibrate trust and correct misinterpretations instantly.
From A UX Perspective
As a UX designer, always being curious to understand how our design approach is changing in the world of AI, I find it essential that we re-evaluate the foundational elements of our craft.
“
By mastering these evolving patterns, like ambient feedback, inline prompts, and transparent AI status indicators, we can ensure that screenless, agent-driven tools remain intuitive, ethical, and deeply human-centered.
Conclusion
The ultimate goal: The best design is no design.
For decades, the digital industry has evaluated software success through engagement metrics like time spent in app, click-through rates, and page views per session. Websites were deliberately engineered to maximise visual engagement and interaction volume.
The philosophy behind Golden Krishna’s seminal book The Best Interface Is No Interface, aligned with the broader Center for Humane Technology’s Time Well Spent movement, turns these metrics on their head. The ultimate test of a modern digital product is no longer how visually captivating its buttons are, but rather: How effectively did this software solve the problem and get out of the user’s way?,
We are entering an era where web applications will no longer be measured by the beauty of their interfaces, but by their ability to render those complex interfaces completely obsolete. The future of the web isn’t more interaction — it is seamless, invisible completion.
results.summary:
Intent-driven design is replacing traditional point-and-click web interfaces with AI-powered systems that execute complex tasks based on user goals rather than manual navigation through menus and forms.

### Key Points
- Intent-driven design shifts software interaction from manual micro-steps to high-level goal expression using natural language.
- Platforms like Perplexity AI, Vercel v0, and Goblin.tools demonstrate how AI can synthesize information, generate code, and organize tasks autonomously.
- The approach relies on three pillars: high-level goal processing, generative UI that adapts to user needs, and autonomous execution by background AI agents.
- Designers are moving away from static layouts toward ambient, context-aware interfaces that prioritize frictionless outcomes over engagement metrics like click-through rates.
- Ethical challenges include the "black box" problem and the need to maintain user control while automating routine digital tasks.

### Why it Matters
This shift represents a fundamental change in how users interact with technology, moving from managing software to achieving outcomes. By prioritizing efficiency over engagement, businesses may see a decline in traditional metrics like time-on-site, but will likely gain significant value through improved user satisfaction and task completion rates.

results.title: Researcher Drops New Microsoft Defender PoC Showing ShieldBreak Patch Can Be Bypassed
results.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
results.content:
The security researcher known as Chaotic Eclipse has dropped a proof-of-concept (PoC) for yet another zero-day in Microsoft Defender.
The vulnerability, codenamed ShieldCrash, is assessed to be a patch bypass for CVE-2026-69414 (CVSS score: 7.8), also called ShieldBreak, which the researcher reported last month.
"Microsoft has failed to properly patch ShieldBreak CVE-2026-69414," Chaotic Eclipse said. "Under specific conditions it is still possible to trigger the exact same problem that was caused by ShieldBreak. While Microsoft fixed several things to prevent re-exploiting the issue, they missed a spot where ShieldBreak can still be exploited."
The PoC demonstrates an arbitrary file read as SYSTEM with the latest version of Windows installed. All supported versions of the desktop operating system are said to be impacted.
The development comes days after Redmond shipped an update to the Microsoft Malware Protection Engine to plug CVE-2026-69414. The issue has been patched in Malware Protection Engine version 1.1.26080.3. It does not require any customer action and does not affect systems that have disabled Microsoft Defender.
"In response to a constantly changing threat landscape, Microsoft frequently updates malware definitions and the Microsoft Malware Protection Engine," the tech giant said. "In order to be effective in helping protect against new and prevalent threats, antimalware software must be kept up to date with these updates in a timely manner."
"For enterprise deployments as well as end users, the default configuration in Microsoft antimalware software helps ensure that malware definitions and the Microsoft Malware Protection Engine are kept up to date automatically. Product documentation also recommends that products are configured for automatic updating."
In recent weeks, Chaotic Eclipse has also released PoC exploits for four vulnerabilities impacting CrowdStrike Falcon Sensor (FalconFlank), Kaspersky (HardBreacher), Avast Antivirus (PrettyPrague), and NVIDIA (GreenSection). Both HardBreacher and PrettyPrague have since been patched by the respective security vendors, while CrowdStrike told The Hacker News that it's investigating the report.
results.summary:
Security researcher Chaotic Eclipse has released a proof-of-concept exploit for a new zero-day vulnerability in Microsoft Defender that bypasses a recent patch for the ShieldBreak security flaw.

### Key Points
- The vulnerability, dubbed ShieldCrash, allows for arbitrary file reads with SYSTEM-level privileges on all supported versions of Windows.
- It functions as a bypass for CVE-2026-69414, a previously identified flaw that Microsoft attempted to fix in Malware Protection Engine version 1.1.26080.3.
- Microsoft maintains that automatic updates for the Malware Protection Engine are the primary defense against such threats for both enterprise and individual users.
- Chaotic Eclipse has recently disclosed similar proof-of-concept exploits for security software from CrowdStrike, Kaspersky, Avast, and NVIDIA.

### Why it Matters
This discovery highlights the ongoing challenge of ensuring complete remediation when security vendors issue patches for complex software vulnerabilities. Users and enterprises must rely on automated update mechanisms to mitigate these risks, as incomplete fixes can leave systems exposed to persistent exploitation.

results.title: The College Students Finding New Ways to Cheat With AI
results.author: Alex Bronzini-Vender
results.content:
At New York University, Introductory Calculus students complete their homework on WebAssign, a platform that promises to make cheating “far more difficult” than using “traditional paper and pen.” But Jared, a sophomore majoring in economics, hasn’t found it especially hard to beat the system. Last semester, a friend of his used an AI coding tool to build a bot that completes his homework. Like a struggling student, the bot moves slowly, leaving a professor checking time stamps none the wiser. Jared’s friend gave it to another friend. And another. He is not sure how many classmates use similar techniques. (The names of students have been changed to let them freely discuss cheating.)
The academic-dishonesty crisis is well documented. When the Harvard Crimson surveyed undergraduates this spring, nearly 40 percent copped to using AI “in ways their instructor may view as inappropriate or against class policy.” Now, schools are scrambling to catch up. Princeton and Oberlin — institutions that have long prided themselves on faith in undergraduates’ morality — are ending the tradition of unsupervised exams. The University of Chicago’s social-sciences division is banning all technology from classrooms in required courses.
But as some faculty move to restrict devices, many administrators are betting on something else: better tech. When California State University system schools upgraded their contracts with Turnitin, a plagiarism-detection giant, campuses paid an additional fee for a tool that scans essays for AI. Columbia University’s Teachers College recommends educators use Draftback, a Chrome extension that lets professors replay a Google doc’s entire revision history. Other institutions have GPTZero, a program that promises to find AI-powered plagiarism with “99 percent accuracy.”
Despite all this, as the fourth academic year of AI college begins, students keep finding innovative ways to skirt the rules. Just a year before Jared’s friend pitted an LLM against WebAssign, agentic coding tools couldn’t yet reverse-engineer the weaknesses in professors’ grading platforms, much less build bespoke software to exploit them. But in the spring of 2025, a new class of AI tools became available to the public. Unlike mere chatbots, newer models can plan multistep tasks, call on external tools like web search and code execution, and carry out complex assignments — from building slide decks to writing and running code — with minimal human supervision.
Educators are often attempting to expose methods of deception that have already been innovated out of existence. The fully AI-generated essay, for instance, is now a relic in Jared’s telling. The paste-and-submit era, he says, “was a few years ago.” There is no use hunting for the word delve and excessive em-dashes. “People are going to find a way to cover up those little stylistic quirks,” Will, who just graduated from Carleton College, tells me. “If the only way you’re trying to discourage cheating is by saying ‘Well, I have a detector,’ then you’re not going to succeed.”
He walked me through the system he’d devised. His professors strictly forbade AI-generated prose — a red line one professor promised to enforce with “a battery” of tools. But stuck during several all-nighters, Will decided to hand Claude his course readings. The LLM wrote the especially challenging bits of an essay, selecting quotes and citing the relevant texts. To evade detection, Will worked back through AI-generated paragraphs, sentence by sentence, rewriting each line.
Theo, a UMass Amherst sophomore, tells me a similar story. The school’s general-education requirements “forced” him into courses “that I just don’t give a fuck about.” (He considers himself an autodidact and would “rather spend that time reading books on things I like.”) For an astronomy midterm — one of those gen-ed requirements — Theo told me he had to submit a ten-minute presentation on a course topic alongside a voice-over script. He delegated it to Codex, OpenAI’s autonomous coding agent, and enhanced the model with Exa, a plug-in upgrading its web-search capabilities. But the draft was unusable: The slides looked too good. So Theo spent roughly four hours restoring the mediocrity of a real college sophomore. “It took a lot of work,” he tells me, to degrade the output. But it was worth it. He got an A.
What struck me, listening to Will and Theo, is how time-consuming cheating seems. Instead of doing their own work, students spend much of their late nights undoing what the models produce. For now, the incentives for students run toward cheating. AI is easy to use and easy enough to hide. But Max Spero, CEO of Pangram Labs — one of the top firms building LLM-writing detectors — believes that if detection tech improves enough, following the rules will become simpler than breaking them. Students reach for AI, he believes, “because it’s so easy and accessible.” If passing off a model’s writing as your own gets harder, students will feel it’s “relatively easier to just do the work themselves.”
In the meantime, many schools have turned to surveillance. Owen, a junior at Princeton familiar with its Honor Committee, says the school often catches AI cheats by spying on internet use. Students’ browsing histories are pulled from the campus network and scanned for recent visits to ChatGPT or Claude. If you whipped out your phone during a quiz, accessing a model on the building’s Wi-Fi, you will likely be busted. While every case requires multiple pieces of evidence, and Princeton says it does not pull students’ search histories unless they are already under investigation, Owen says the network logs have become critical in proving academic dishonesty. Every case he’s been aware of lately has leaned on them.
Still, whether you get investigated at all is a crapshoot, he says: It “varies widely depending on the class, the professor, and how much they personally know about generative AI.” Across the university, he adds, “enforcement’s behind the ball.”
Rather than aim an arsenal of high-tech surveillance methods at students, some professors have opted for low-tech solutions. Danielle Carr, a historian and anthropologist at UCLA, largely won’t assign writing unless she can watch her students do it. They will parse texts and fill out notebooks in “reading jail,” where graduate students supervise their work. AI, Carr thinks, is not “a technical problem that has a technical fix.” As long as students want to dupe their professors, they’ll always out-engineer the tools built to stop them. (She is also hesitant to become reliant on “invasive surveillance” tech, which “opens doors to some very creepy shit.”)
The solution, she believes, might be upstream from mere enforcement. To stop AI cheating, “you have to inspire love” of learning, Carr tells me. “Perhaps it is naïve to be like, Everyone should just be a more ethical and excellent teacher and transmit the love and passion that you have — but that’s how I feel.”
From afar, the modern university can look like a liars’ haven. But the students I interviewed insist that they still want to learn. Theo doesn’t use AI in classes he cares about; Jared values “being able to think for myself”; Will tells me he has a “visceral” distaste for AI-generated prose. A liberal-arts education promises that a class, and its toil, changes you for the better. But Jared, Theo, and Will don’t seem to think many of their classes do — and more surveillance probably won’t change their minds. At some point, colleges and educators will have to answer that skepticism by proving that using AI for an assignment is not worth it.
If higher education loses the struggle against AI, Carr believes, it won’t be for want of solutions. “If your wife is having an affair with the milkman,” she says, “it’s not that it’s so confusing about what to do.” It’s just that “the solutions would be pretty annoying.”
results.summary:
College students are increasingly using advanced AI tools to bypass academic integrity measures, forcing universities to choose between invasive surveillance technologies and fundamental changes to their teaching methods.

### Key Points
- Students are utilizing autonomous AI agents and coding tools to automate homework and bypass platforms like WebAssign and Turnitin.
- Institutions including Princeton, Oberlin, and the University of Chicago are responding by banning technology or ending unsupervised exams.
- Universities are investing in detection software like GPTZero and Draftback, though students frequently manually edit AI outputs to evade these systems.
- Some educators, such as UCLA’s Danielle Carr, are shifting toward "reading jail" environments where students complete all work under direct supervision.
- Princeton and other schools are increasingly relying on campus network logs to track student access to generative AI platforms during exams.

### Why it Matters
The ongoing arms race between AI-assisted cheating and detection technology highlights a growing disconnect between traditional academic requirements and student engagement. If universities cannot prove the intrinsic value of their coursework, they risk losing the battle for academic integrity regardless of how much they invest in surveillance.

results.title: Rushes | Remembering Dolly Parton, A24 Teases Nathan Fielder's Elizabeth Holmes Doc, the 100 Most-Screened Films in NYC
results.author: Notebook
results.content:
Get in touch to send in cinephile news and discoveries. To keep up with our latest features, sign up for the Weekly Edit newsletter and follow us @mubinotebook on X and Instagram.
NEWS
- Meryl Streep and Laura Poitras have come aboard as executive producers on Julia Loktev’s upcoming documentary My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile (2026), the second part of Loktev’s profile of independent Russian journalists operating in the wake of the invasion of Ukraine, which recently had its world premiere at the Venice Film Festival. In a statement, Streep describes Loktev as “the Samuel Pepys of Putin’s Russia” and describes her films as a “blazing achievement.”
- Two surprises have recently happened on the festival circuit. The first is that Luca Guadagnino’s Artificial (2026), which was dropped by Amazon MGM Studios in June, will have its world premiere at the New York Film Festival followed by a Gala screening at the London Film Festival. Secondly, the Telluride Film Festival’s secret screening was revealed to be Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s three-hour documentary You Can See Everything (2026) about Elizabeth Holmes.
- AMC has launched its own distribution company, Leawood Films, which will focus on “small and mid-budget sized movies” from “emerging and established filmmakers.” This arrives on the heels of the success of Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour (2023), which AMC directly released into theaters after striking a deal with the eponymous popstar.
- Television presenter and YouTube personality Chris Hansen has purchased preshow advertising before every screening of Lance Oppenheim’s psychological thriller Primetime (2026), which chronicles Hansen’s tenure hosting To Catch a Predator (2004–07). The ad reportedly directs viewers to Hansen’s streaming network TruBlu where he continues his predator investigations.
DEVELOPING
- Lea Seydoux and Bill Murray are set to star in Ursula Meier’s The Quiet Land, which is reportedly influenced by the work of Swiss police photographer Arnold Odermatt, and will be lensed by Agnès Godard.
- Renate Reinsve is set to star as Mary Wollstonecraft in Mia Hansen-Løve’s If Love Should Die, which chronicles the last twelve years of the English writer and philosopher’s life amidst the French Revolution.
REMEMBERING
- Dolly Parton has died at 80. The American singer-songwriter and actress achieved initial success in country music by appearing on the weekly variety series The Porter Wagoner Show (1960–81) beginning in the late-1960s. She and Wagoner became a popular duo for nearly ten years before Parton pursued a thriving solo career. In between touring and releasing hit studio records, she starred in her own variety series Dolly! (1976–77), made frequent appearances on The Tonight Show Starring Johnny Carson (1962–92) that boosted her popularity, and co-starred in many television specials headlined by Mac Davis and Cher. She made her feature film debut in 9 to 5 (1980) and wrote the film’s theme song, which was nominated for both an Oscar and a Grammy. She went on to star in a string of films over the next decade: The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas (1982), Rhinestone (1984), Steel Magnolias (1989), and Straight Talk (1992). Up until her death, she continued to regularly appear on television in made-for-TV films and sitcom cameos. Her final film was the Emmy-award winning musical drama Dolly Parton’s Christmas on the Square (2020), for which she produced and wrote the music. “I never knew anyone like her,” remembered former costar Jane Fonda. “She was simultaneously a naughty, playful southern gal from the hollows of Tennessee and a deep, soulful thinker who could see through people right down to their true selves.”
- Tim Curry has died at 80. The English actor quickly garnered international recognition for his performance as Dr. Frank-N-Furter in both The Rocky Horror Show stage production and its 1975 film adaptation. Curry went on to have a prolific career on screen and stage, moving easily between live-action and voice roles. Some of his most memorable live-action film performances include Wadsworth in Clue (1985), Dr. Yevgeniy Petrov in The Hunt for Red October (1990), and Mr. Hector in Home Alone 2: Lost in New York. He also received praise for his turns as Pennywise the Clown in the two-part miniseries It (1990) and Nigel Thornberry in the animated series The Wild Thornberrys (1998–2004). Along with regularly performing on stage, racking up accolades for playing Mozart in Amadeus and King Arthur in Spamalot, he also released three rock albums, voiced numerous audiobooks, and continued to reprise Dr. Frank-N-Furter for various charity and anniversary events. “I don’t fear death,” Curry said a year prior. “I try to avoid it, as I think we all do. But, I suspect that in the end, I will welcome it.”
RECOMMENDED READING
- “The category is a capacious one, encompassing reclusive geniuses, thwarted iconoclasts, and tragic shooting stars. Some of these artists make only one movie. Some make more but resist the temptations of a prolific career, because of their own exacting standards, the challenge of raising money to make films, or forces beyond their control … In all cases, though, the scarcity of the films combines with the often distinctive nature of the work to capture our collective imagination, giving the reticent auteur a magnetism that, while not exactly unearned, also speaks to our own attitudes toward the creative act.” For The Yale Review, Bilge Ebiri examines various “reticent auteurs,” including Charles Laughton, Barbara Loden, and Víctor Erice, and their unique value in an increasingly algorithm-driven economy.
- “The Chronovisor is a hauntological invention, and in her research, Dr. Courte has cause to bring dead tech back to life. In one case she reassembles a video, detangling and manually winding a snarl of magnetic tape. She also watches a segment of the French-Canadian TV newsmagazine Camera ’89 profiling François Brune, a French priest and collaborator of Ernetti, who made his own attempts to use technology to rouse the dead. The media is the medium, though the message is garbled: When Camera ’89 plays a tape of Brune’s, the speech is raspy, barking, an almost entirely incoherent squawk to match the quality of the tape itself. An aura of unreality grows around the subject as information becomes sparser; things that were once common knowledge fade into irrelevance and dispute.” For The Baffler, Mark Asch reviews Kevin Walker and Jack Auen’s Chronovisor (2026) and how it fits within and exemplifies the “academic mystery movie.”
- “[Will] Gluck’s touch is very light, but the movie’s obsession with credibility means most characters we get to meet stop to point out their dislike for the law. Whoever supports this thing is kept carefully offscreen. At most, we get a drunken rockstar going into a ramble about maybe the conservatives had a point because this makes who you pick to spend the night with special, right before getting increasingly creepier and falling into his face. The most chilling moment comes early when Turner remarks that most of his friends got married the previous year, the implication being that they just settled into marriage for convenient intimacy. The real crime is the one against the romantic comedy promise: you are not supposed to marry to find a fuck buddy.” On his Substack, Filipe Furtado unpacks the recent high-concept rom-com One Night Only (2026) and how it embodies the fictions Hollywood loves to tell.
- “The pre-Hitler mood captured in M (1931) finds an echo in films like Civil War (2024) and One Battle After Another (2025). Conflict no longer appears as a temporary crisis but as a permanent condition; politics becomes an endless chain of confrontations rather than a system capable of resolution. Like M, these films imagine a world of eroding norms and ambient violence. Kracauer’s warning, reaching across decades, is not that such outcomes are inevitable but that when a society begins to normalize this atmosphere, it grows more susceptible to the promises of demagogues—and to the conflicts that follow.” For The New Republic, Jimmy So looks back at Siegfried Kracauer’s landmark text From Caligari to Hitler and how the author’s diagnostician lens can be deployed in a contemporary context.
RECOMMENDED EVENTS
- Berlin, through September 24: The Arsenal Institute for Film and Video Art presents Here and Now – The Films of Christoph Hochhäusler, a retrospective of the German filmmaker’s films tied to an exhibition of his materials at the Neuer Berliner Kunstverein.
- Turin, through October 5: The National Museum of Cinema presents My Name Is Orson Welles, which features more than four hundred items across many public and private collections dedicated to the auteur that retrace his unique life and career.
- New York, September 17 through October 13: The Museum of Modern Art presents Yuen Woo-ping: The Number One Martial Arts Director Under the Sky, a retrospective of the filmmaker and action choreographer’s work, from Drunken Master (1978) through Ip Man 4: The Finale (2019).
- Amsterdam, September 19 through January 31: Eye Filmmuseum presents Ulrich Seidl – On Life, Love, and Death, the first exhibition, and a complete retrospective, of the Austrian director’s work in the Netherlands.
RECOMMENDED VIEWING
- A24 presents a surprise teaser for Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s new documentary You Can See Everything (2026), which follows disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes as she prepares to go to prison.
- Neon presents a trailer for Fjord (2026), Cristian Mungiu’s Palme d’Or-winning legal thriller starring Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve as a couple fighting for the custody of their children after their behavior comes under scrutiny by the government.
- Magnolia Pictures presents a trailer for The History of Concrete (2026), John Wilson’s feature-length debut about the documentarian’s efforts to make a documentary about concrete using a Hallmark-approved commercial formula.
- Neon presents a trailer for Once Upon a Time in Harlem (2026), a documentary about a 1972 gathering of the surviving members of the Harlem Renaissance at Duke Ellington’s townhouse, originally shot by William Greaves and completed by his son David.
RECENTLY ON NOTEBOOK
- “Markopoulos wrote that ending a film is like tying an intricate surgical knot. One must make ‘the best knot for each work; and it is completed forever.’ It must be clean. It is somewhere near three in the morning when the projection cuts off and, though abrupt, there is a sense of finality. Before the screening, Beavers had asked that when the Temenos ends, we hold a moment of silence. These few minutes of quiet are like a canopy. In the dark, in the absence of the projector’s hum, true silence takes on a thick feeling in the air. The screen loses its violet wash as eyes readjust. We wait, until Beavers releases a thunderous ‘Thank you.’” Emma Fuchs reports on the screening of the final four cycles of Gregory J. Markopoulos’s Eniaios (1948–90), the culmination of the Greek-American experimental filmmaker's magnum opus.
- “The launch of Video Home System (VHS) in the mid-1970s therefore came at the perfect time for Northern Ireland’s cinema lovers, who desired entertainment and escapism but were less willing than ever to leave the comfort and relative safety of their own homes … For the time, the power to control when audiences watched films began to shift from the exhibitors to the audience. Power shifted, too, from producers to consumers, and for the first time people could directly record films or television programs onto blank tapes and play, pause, or rewind at their own leisure.” Sam Manning explores the VHS boom in Northern Ireland during the Troubles, when cinemagoing “became less of a social habit and more of an occasional activity that carried a level of potential risk.”
- “The Samurai and the Prisoner (2026) is set apart from these other works by virtue of its assertive and imperative qualities. Whereas Kurosawa’s past filmography has sought to elucidate, The Samurai and the Prisoner seeks to prescribe—a shift perhaps commensurate with advancing age and stature (an impulse that finds more satirical expression in the coda of Cloud [2024], which ends with a character offering advice). Murashige is seemingly a self-portrait of sorts for Kurosawa, and after decades of diagnosing the ills of a modern world defined by alienation—and putting his observations in literally or figuratively scarifying terms—the filmmaker now wishes to push, calmly but urgently, for a fundamental, structural change.” Alexis Moon examines The Samurai and the Prisoner in the context of Kiyoshi Kurosawa’s career and how the Japanese director has charted a new path with his latest period drama.
- “The contrast with General Muhammad Zia-ul Haq, who overthrew Bhutto in a 1977 military coup and later executed him, has often produced a simplified narrative: of a liberal cultural sphere abruptly replaced by sweeping repression under his ‘Islamization’ drive. Yet Aina (1977) remained in cinemas for a record 401 weeks, well into the Zia period. Censorship until Zia’s death in 1988 undoubtedly affected filmmakers and narrowed the visual grammar of romance, but the shift was uneven rather than absolute: While romancing in an elevator became increasingly unlikely, lovers still had their duets. Far from a total and lasting capture by moral conservatism, post-Zia cinema in the 1990s often turned to overt sexualization to draw audiences back into a struggling exhibition economy.” Manahil Tahira unpacks the legacy of Nazrul Islam’s Aina and the history of erotic depictions within Pakistani culture.
WISH LIST
- The Philosophy of Time Travel: The Epic Sequel to the Motion Picture Donnie Darko, Richard Kelly’s literary follow-up to his 2001 debut feature is available to preorder.
- Rachel Antonoff presents a “Second Coming” T-shirt inspired by Mona Fastvold’s musical drama The Testament of Ann Lee (2025).
EXTRAS
- Screen Slate compiled a list of the 100 most-screened films in New York City across the last fifteen years, sorted by the number of individual screenings, including a column for showtimes.

results.title: Holtec Nuclear Targets $10.2 Billion Valuation in Nasdaq IPO
results.author: Charles Kennedy
results.content:
Holtec Nuclear Corporation is seeking a valuation of up to $10.2 billion in its planned Nasdaq debut, putting one of the largest privately held U.S. nuclear technology businesses in front of public-market investors during a surge in interest in nuclear power.
The Camden, New Jersey-based company plans to sell 50 million Class A shares at between $15 and $18 each, according to its latest regulatory filing. At the top of that range, Holtec would raise $900 million in gross proceeds.
The $10.2 billion valuation reflects the top-end offering price and roughly 566.7 million shares on a fully exchanged basis following the transaction. At the $16.50 midpoint of the range, the equivalent valuation would be about $9.35 billion.
Underwriters also have an option to purchase another 7.5 million shares, which could lift gross proceeds above $1 billion if exercised in full at the $18 offering price. Holtec expects approximately $775.2 million in net proceeds at the midpoint, or $893.1 million if the additional-share option is fully exercised.
Holtec said the money will be available for general corporate purposes including accelerating licensing and deployment of its SMR-300 small modular reactor, expanding manufacturing capacity and commercializing other energy technologies.
That puts Holtec's reactor ambitions at the center of the investment case. The company plans to build its first two SMR-300 units, known as Pioneer One and Pioneer Two, at the Palisades nuclear site in Michigan. The two-reactor project would provide up to 680 MW of capacity, with Holtec targeting commercial operation in the early 2030s.
Before then, Holtec is attempting another major nuclear milestone at Palisades. The company is working to return the roughly 800-MW conventional reactor to service after it permanently shut in May 2022. Holtec expects the restart in 2026; if completed, it would be the first previously decommissioned U.S. commercial nuclear plant to return to operation.
The project has substantial government support, including a U.S. Department of Energy loan guarantee facility of up to $1.52 billion. Holtec has also secured long-term power purchase agreements for Palisades, giving the company a prospective source of power-generation revenue in addition to its established nuclear equipment and services operations.
Holtec's IPO comes as nuclear power attracts renewed capital amid expectations for sharply higher electricity demand from data centers, artificial intelligence and broader electrification. Nuclear companies including X-energy and Standard Nuclear have already entered the public markets through traditional IPOs this year, while Westinghouse has also reportedly taken steps toward a potential U.S. listing.

- Proceeds will fund the deployment of the SMR-300 small modular reactor and the expansion of manufacturing capacity for energy technologies.
- The company is working to restart the 800-MW Palisades nuclear plant in Michigan by 2026, supported by a $1.52 billion Department of Energy loan guarantee.
- The Palisades site is slated to host the first two SMR-300 units, Pioneer One and Pioneer Two, with commercial operations targeted for the early 2030s.
- The IPO follows a surge in investor interest in nuclear power driven by rising electricity demand from artificial intelligence and data center operations.

### Why it Matters
This public offering highlights the growing role of nuclear energy in meeting the massive power requirements of the modern technology sector. By securing capital for both reactor restarts and modular technology, Holtec is positioning itself as a central player in the transition toward carbon-free, high-capacity electricity generation.

results.title: EU auditors say AI is helping tobacco smugglers pick their next target
results.author: Ana-Maria Stanciuc
results.content:
The European Court of Auditors has published two findings that sit awkwardly together. The EU has no reliable picture of the size or structure of its illicit tobacco market.
The criminal networks running that market, according to the auditor who led the report, are using artificial intelligence to work out where to move next.
Special report 23/2026, published on Wednesday under the title “Combating the illicit trade in tobacco in the EU: fragmented efforts and persistent gaps”, estimates the annual cost to EU and national budgets at €13bn. Roughly one in 10 cigarettes made in the bloc is smuggled or produced illegally.
Petri Sarvamaa, the report’s reporting member, made the technology point in an interview with EUobserver.
“Artificial intelligence has hugely benefited the criminals because they can very easily find out where to move next,” he said, describing organisations that track enforcement activity across member states and analyse where the loopholes are.
Strip the acronym out and what he is describing is an information advantage. Smuggling has always depended on knowing which border is loosely staffed, which member state has the softest excise regime and which enforcement agency is looking elsewhere this month.
What has changed is how cheap it now is to assemble that picture from public sources and keep it current. The auditors’ other finding is what makes this uncomfortable:
“We do not have an EU-wide picture of the true size, structure, and economic impact of this illegal market,” Sarvamaa said.
One side of this contest has invested in data infrastructure. It is not the regulator.
What the report does not do is say how any of this was established, which is the gap a technology desk should notice.
Sarvamaa’s claim about AI came in an interview rather than in the audit, and from what is visible of the document it names no tools, no cases and no seized systems.
That does not make it wrong. Enforcement officials across Europe have been describing the same shift for a year.
But an assertion that criminal groups have operationalised AI is the kind of claim that hardens into received wisdom without ever acquiring evidence, and auditors are supposed to be the people who insist on the difference.
The scale is not theoretical. Belgian investigators found a factory running machines capable of about 1 million cigarettes an hour. The largest plant dismantled in Spain yielded 3 million counterfeit packets.
Alongside cigarettes, the report counts nearly 21,000 tonnes of illicit non-cigarette tobacco. The EU’s anti-fraud office prevented €178mn in lost tax revenue last year, which, set against a €13bn annual estimate, gives the ratio the auditors are complaining about.
Their diagnosis is institutional rather than technological. Coordination is fragmented, enforcement is uneven between member states, information exchange is inconsistent, and there is no harmonised EU law covering the trade.
Those are the conditions that make cross-border arbitrage worth analysing in the first place. An organisation that can see all 27 jurisdictions at once has an obvious advantage over 27 authorities that cannot see each other.
The product mix is shifting too. Vapes and heated tobacco now account for about 13% of the illicit market by value, a category that barely existed when the enforcement architecture was designed and one whose supply chains run through the same e-commerce and logistics rails as legitimate consumer electronics.
“That is €13bn that never reaches our schools, hospitals, or other public services,” Sarvamaa said of the revenue loss.
The number is worth treating with the same caution the auditors apply to it, since it derives from external studies rather than direct measurement, which is precisely the measurement problem the report is complaining about.
An institution that cannot size the market cannot size its losses either, and the honest version of this report is a request to be allowed to find out.

results.summary:
The European Court of Auditors reports that criminal networks are using artificial intelligence to exploit fragmented enforcement, costing EU member states an estimated €13 billion in annual revenue.

### Key Points
- The European Court of Auditors report, "Combating the illicit trade in tobacco in the EU," estimates annual tax losses at €13 billion.
- Approximately one in 10 cigarettes consumed within the European Union is produced or smuggled illegally.
- Criminal organizations are reportedly using artificial intelligence to identify enforcement loopholes and optimize smuggling routes across 27 member states.
- Illicit vapes and heated tobacco products now represent 13% of the illegal market by value.
- Auditors identified significant institutional gaps, including inconsistent information exchange and a lack of harmonized laws across the bloc.
- The EU’s anti-fraud office recovered €178 million in lost tax revenue last year, a small fraction of the total estimated losses.

### Why it Matters
The report highlights a critical information asymmetry where criminal syndicates utilize advanced data analytics to outpace uncoordinated national enforcement agencies. This institutional failure threatens public budgets and complicates efforts to regulate emerging tobacco products like vapes.

results.title: Apple Store is down ahead of iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone Duo foldable and more announcements
results.author: Benjamin Mayo
results.content:
Following the usual tradition, the Apple Store is down ahead of this morning’s September Apple event, kicking off at 10 AM Pacific Time.
We are expecting Apple to announce the new iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, the foldable iPhone Duo, Apple Watch Series 12, and updated AirPods (fifth-generation).
This is the first event led by new CEO John Ternus, who has a bunch of new products to announce including the debut of the folding iPhone Duo.
The Duo will have a ~5.5-inch outer display when closed, and a ~7.8-inch display when opened up, a bit smaller than an iPad mini in size. The Duo’s big screen, when unfolded, enables immersive media experiences, and more productivity with split-screen multitasking of two apps at once.
Apple is expected to differentiate itself from other foldables on the market by focusing on premium build quality, including a custom-designed hinge. The crease along the center of the inner screen is expected to be minimal.
The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max will also be launched today, including new processors, improved camera system, and a new cherry red color option. The Dynamic Island on the new Pro models is shrinking in width, resulting in even less bezel. The starting price of the 18 Pro line is anticipated to rise by about $100.
The base model iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2 will not make an appearance at this event. Apple is shifting the release schedule, so the entry-level iPhone will no longer launch in the fall. Instead, we expect it to arrive in the spring. Apple will presumably keep selling the base iPhone 17 until then.
Also today, we expect unveilings of the new Apple Watch lineup, Series 12 and Ultra 4, and new AirPods 5. The new Watches will reportedly include revamped health tracking functionality and a new AI feature that generates recaps of your daily whereabouts and conversations.
Other upcoming new Apple hardware includes a smart home display product, Apple TV and HomePod mini refreshes, and a MacBook Pro featuring an OLED touch screen. Most reports indicate these products will launch later in the year, likely as part of an October event.
9to5Mac is on the ground in Cupertino today, and we will have live coverage of all the iPhone announcements as they happen — so stay tuned for all the latest.
results.summary:
Apple has taken its online store offline ahead of today’s September event, where CEO John Ternus will debut the foldable iPhone Duo, iPhone 18 Pro, and new wearables.

### Key Points
- Apple is launching the foldable iPhone Duo, featuring a 7.8-inch inner display and a custom-designed hinge to minimize screen creasing.
- The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max will introduce new processors, an improved camera system, a cherry red color, and a narrower Dynamic Island.
- Starting prices for the iPhone 18 Pro lineup are expected to increase by approximately $100.
- The event includes the unveiling of Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, which feature new AI-driven health tracking and daily recap capabilities.
- Apple is shifting its release schedule, moving the launch of entry-level iPhone models to the spring instead of the traditional fall window.

This event marks a significant strategic shift for Apple under new CEO John Ternus, particularly with the introduction of the company's first foldable device. results.content:
Apple is set to unveil its first foldable iPhone on Wednesday, September 9, at the company's "Surprise and Shine" event beginning at 10:00 a.m. Pacific Time, and a last-minute leak from Bloomberg's Mark Gurman has revealed some key details about the foldable.
- Foldable iPhone name: Previous rumors and reports have clung to the name "iPhone Ultra" for Apple's first foldable iPhone – a name that Gurman himself has used several times in the past. However, in his latest report, Gurman says Apple has settled on the name "iPhone Duo" for the device.
- Base storage: A rumor from back in March suggested the foldable iPhone would have a base storage capacity of 256GB, with 512GB and 1TB options also available. Gurman's latest report corroborates the base 256GB storage option. While his report doesn't mention the other two storage options, it seems likely they will define two higher price points.
- Starting price: TrendForce estimates and other reports have suggested the iPhone Duo will start at above $2,000, and perhaps go as high as $2,500. Gurman's latest report says the starting price will be $2,000 for the 256GB model, while the highest-capacity model will be around $3,000.
- Color options: Previous rumors suggested Apple would "stay away from fun colors" for its first foldable iPhone, with a darker color being described as a shade of indigo rather than black. Gurman's last-minute report backs up that idea, saying the iPhone Duo will come in white and dark blue.

results.title: Cable News Bundling Hits The App Store; Grindr’s Turn On The Data Sales Hot Seat
results.author: AdExchanger
results.content:
What Now?
Cable network MS NOW, previously MSNBC, launched a subscription app this week at $7.99 per month or $79.99 annually.
News media has struggled to find its place in the mobile subscription economy. (CNN+, anyone?)
Behemoths like Walmart, Uber and Amazon commonly bundle their offerings with entertainment studios and other content providers, but never with pure news publishers. Netflix avoids news programming like the plague.
But MS NOW is trying to break that pattern. It’s got its own marketing bundle-partners, including a deal with meditation app Calm, for instance, Variety reports.
And beyond bundling, MS NOW is also leaning into direct engagement as a hook. One unique selling point is that its subscribers get regular live Q&A access to news anchors ahead of their shows, including before Rachel Maddow’s weekly Monday program and the “Morning Joe Family Meeting.”
Given the likely small subscriber base and the fact that only a fraction will join any given live Q&A, the feature effectively gives a handful of superfans a direct line to inform or even shape those programs.
Inviting subscribers into the editorial process is a fresh conflict of interest. Then again, the old editorial/advertising firewalls are already eroding now that marketers and Big Tech platforms treat news as a political and brand-safety liability.
An Axe To Grindr
LGBTQ+ hookup app Grindr prides itself on its anonymity and discretion.
So it’s not exactly a great look that the company will now pay $35 million to settle a UK lawsuit alleging that it sold user data – including HIV-positive status – to advertisers.
The lawsuit covers the period prior to Grindr’s 2020 acquisition by investment group San Vicente Acquisition LLC. It claimed users believed their personal information would only be shared internally with app users, but was instead sold to ad targeting companies including Localytics and Apptimize.
Grindr’s current VC ownership denies any wrongdoing and is admitting no liability as part of the settlement, CBC reports. However, the company says it “recognizes and acknowledges the distress and loss of trust expressed by some of its UK users regarding that pre-2020 period.”
“Distress and loss of trust” is putting it mildly. The idea that sensitive data – such as a person’s LGBTQ+ status or health information like an HIV diagnosis – could be shared with third parties without their consent is an oft-cited hypothetical nightmare scenario. Well, it happened.
But Grindr is only just the latest example of a company allegedly (gotta say “allegedly!”) playing fast and loose with user data when there’s money to be made, and then paying a hefty fine to avoid further scrutiny. Unfortunately, it won’t be the last.
Taking The L(G)
Just a few months after reporting that some LG monitors push unwanted ads to users, PC hardware review outlet Gamers Nexus now claims that LG television sets are able to record audio from the on-device microphones if hacked in a particular way, The Verge reports.
According to Gamers Nexus, which partnered with Level1Techs and independent security researchers, LG TVs can scan Wi-Fi networks for nearby devices and location data, and record microphone audio even when they’re on standby or disconnected from the internet.
The investigation also cites LG’s automatic content recognition (ACR) technology, which uses audio and visual signals to identify what’s playing on a screen.
ACR is nothing new. Most modern smart TVs use similar technology to identify the content and commercials people are watching, although outside of the ad tech industry, the majority of casual viewers have never heard of it.
This investigation is changing that, which could prove awkward for LG. The Gamers Nexus YouTube audience may have been largely unfamiliar with ACR before, but they’re savvy enough to be outraged by its privacy implications.
But Wait! There’s More!
OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar wants ChatGPT’s ads business to be like “if Google and Meta had a baby.” [Business Insider]
Agencies react to the FTC’s suit against Amazon alleging that the platform illegally manipulated its ad auction – and their response is a near-unanimous “meh.” [Digiday]
The Department of Homeland Security operates a predictive policing unit that analyzes the financial data of Americans and feeds it to local police so they can pull over anyone the government thinks is worth searching. [404 Media]
Despite rolling out new AI detection tools, Meta has let hundreds more CSAM ads run across its platforms – including some with photos of real children. [Wired]
In related news, Meta’s history of privacy violations and lack of consumer trust might hurt adoption of its new Muse AI assistant. [TechCrunch]
You’re Hired!
Commerce media platform Fluent names Jeanniey Walden as CMO. [release]
“Decisioning economics” startup Precise hires Dave Antonelli as CRO and Jordan Cauley as CTO. [release]
Multicultural media and marketing company My Code appoints a new CRO, COO and CFO. [Adweek]
Thanks for reading AdExchanger’s Daily News Roundup. Want it by email? Sign up here.
results.summary:
MS NOW launches a subscription app with unique anchor access, while Grindr settles a UK data privacy lawsuit for $35 million and LG faces scrutiny over smart TV surveillance.

### Key Points
- MS NOW introduced a subscription service priced at $7.99 monthly, featuring exclusive live Q&A sessions with news anchors like Rachel Maddow.
- Grindr agreed to a $35 million settlement regarding allegations that it shared sensitive user data, including HIV status, with third-party advertisers before 2020.
- Security researchers discovered that LG smart TVs can record audio and track location data via automatic content recognition technology, even while in standby mode.
- OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar is reportedly developing an advertising strategy for ChatGPT that combines the data-driven models of Google and Meta.
- Meta continues to face criticism for allowing ads containing child sexual abuse material to run on its platforms despite implementing new AI detection tools.

### Why it Matters
These developments highlight the growing tension between corporate data monetization strategies and consumer privacy expectations across media, social, and hardware sectors. As companies integrate more invasive tracking and advertising technologies, they face increasing regulatory scrutiny and potential reputational damage from users and security researchers.

results.title: 4 Bose Speakers You Can Buy With Built-In Voice Assistants
results.author: staff@bgr.com (Jonathan Sayers)
results.content:
4 Bose Speakers You Can Buy With Built-In Voice Assistants
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
Even though some audiophiles hate Bose, there's no denying that this company manufactures some quality products. There are even several Bose speakers with top scores from Consumer Reports. Not all of them have built-in voice assistants, though. If you're looking for a smart speaker that can serve as the voice-controlled hub for your entertainment needs, it's important to buy one that has native compatibility with Alexa or Google Assistant.
To help you find the right Bose speaker for your next smart home upgrade, we made a list of four well-rated options. Each of these speakers has built-in compatibility with Alexa, Google Assistant, or both, but keep in mind that you will have to choose one or the other during the speaker's initial setup. You can always change your preferred voice assistant later using the Voice Settings option in the Bose Music app. A full explanation of how we chose these speakers is included at the end of this article.
Lifestyle Ultra Speaker
The Bose Lifestyle Ultra Speaker is a versatile model you can buy for $299. Bose asserts that it has "room-filling performance" that provides clear sound even if you're far away. This makes it a solid choice as your main voice assistant hub, because you can get the full experience of listening or giving commands even if you're actively moving through the room. The Lifestyle Ultra can be placed on a tabletop or mounted to a stand or wall, giving you flexibility.
The Lifestyle series of speakers are also the first Bose products to launch with Alexa+ built in, so the Lifestyle Ultra can provide more sophisticated services compared to other Bose speakers. You could ask for curated song suggestions or have natural conversations with your digital assistant, for example. The advanced Alexa+ service is free for Amazon Prime members, but even if you don't have Prime, Alexa+ is actually worth paying for because it can improve the overall capability of your entire smart home.
Portable Smart Speaker
The Bose Portable Smart Speaker, as its name implies, is designed to go anywhere. The handle makes it easy to carry with you, and its cylindrical design allows for 360-degree sound for immersive listening without stressing over optimal placement. It's also rated for IPX4 water resistance, which means that it's completely safe to use outdoors around splashing water. At a list price of $399, which you may find discounted often, the portability and durability may come at a premium cost.
Its built-in support for Alexa and Google Assistant lets you issue voice commands while on the go, as long as you have a Wi-Fi or a mobile connection. There are many clever ways to use smart speakers in your home, but the Bose Portable Smart Speaker lets you bring those conveniences with you outside the home too. Of course, the Portable Smart Speaker is also viable for an at-home listening experience, especially in smaller rooms. It's designed to be capable of broader smart home integration, and some buyers claim it beats competitor smart speakers in quality.
Smart Soundbar
The Bose Smart Soundbar can be a solid addition to your home theater setup for the price of $429. We compared Bose and Marshall as speaker brands and found that Bose stands out for having a more comprehensive soundbar lineup. In particular, experts praise the Bose Smart Soundbar for having a wide Dolby Atmos soundstage, low audio latency, and an AI-powered dialogue boost mode that helps on-screen character voices stand out.
You can control the Bose Smart Soundbar using Alexa or Bose's proprietary Voice4Video technology. You can also use Google Chromecast to wirelessly connect other devices to the soundbar without relying on Bluetooth. However, Google Assistant is not available as a built-in voice control option for this product. Even so, the voice command options that are available can help you enjoy big-screen entertainment more seamlessly. Just keep in mind that the Bose Smart Soundbar lacks support for the DTS surround sound standard.
Lifestyle Ultra Soundbar
The Bose Lifestyle Ultra Soundbar is an even more luxurious speaker for your home theater, coming in at a premium price of $1,099. It's the successor to the Bose Smart Ultra Soundbar, which was already one of the best soundbars you can buy in 2026. As part of Bose's all-new Lifestyle lineup, though, this latest iteration comes with Alexa+ support and has seamless compatibility with the rest of Bose's modular Lifestyle ecosystem.
What makes the Lifestyle Ultra Soundbar worth considering, even at more than twice the price of other Bose speakers, is versatility. Reviews have highlighted a wide range of playback options and sound levels to suit rooms of any size. It also demonstrates great audio clarity for music, speech, and other elements in the soundscape. As a hub for your digital voice assistant, the Lifestyle Ultra Soundbar provides all the functionality third-party speakers offer, especially if you opt to pay for access to Alexa+.
How we selected these Bose smart speakers
When we created this list of Bose smart speakers, we only chose products that have built-in voice assistant compatibility without the need to connect them to an intermediary device. We also only named speakers you can actually buy; we did not include discontinued products like the Bose Home Speaker 300 or Home Speaker 500, despite the former popularity of those products and their native voice assistant features.
For this list, we only recommended Bose speakers that are readily available from retailers like Amazon and that you can start controlling with voice commands after a simple out-of-the-box setup process. Furthermore, each product on this list holds an Amazon customer rating above 3.5 stars at the time of this writing, with no frequent defects reported throughout Amazon user reviews.
results.summary:
Bose offers a range of high-quality speakers and soundbars featuring built-in voice assistant compatibility, allowing users to integrate smart home controls directly into their audio entertainment systems.

### Key Points
- The $299 Lifestyle Ultra Speaker features Alexa+ for advanced conversational capabilities and curated music suggestions.
- Priced at $399, the Portable Smart Speaker offers 360-degree sound, IPX4 water resistance, and support for both Alexa and Google Assistant.
- The $429 Smart Soundbar includes Dolby Atmos, AI-powered dialogue enhancement, and Voice4Video technology for home theater setups.
- The premium $1,099 Lifestyle Ultra Soundbar serves as a modular hub with Alexa+ support and high-fidelity audio for various room sizes.
- All selected models maintain an Amazon customer rating above 3.5 stars and require no intermediary devices for voice control functionality.

### Why it Matters
Integrating voice-controlled speakers into a home ecosystem allows for seamless management of entertainment and smart devices through simple verbal commands. Choosing hardware with native assistant support ensures a more reliable and responsive user experience compared to relying on external bridge devices.
